lessons.title: Dendrites compute: nonlinear integration inside a single neuron
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to explain in biophysical terms why a cortical pyramidal neuron is not a point summing device, say what a dendritic spike and a dendritic plateau potential are, and sort the evidence into what has been measured, what has been modelled, and what has been argued.

Begin with the textbook baseline. In the standard account a presynaptic action potential produces a postsynaptic potential of a definable size, and the neuron sums those potentials over space and time to decide whether to fire. Section 6.3 of the UTHealth textbook Synaptic Transmission in the Central Nervous System makes the arithmetic explicit: the synaptic potential at the skeletal neuromuscular junction is about 50 mV, whereas an action potential in a spinal 1A afferent produces a potential of only about 1 mV in a spinal motor neuron, a fifty-fold difference. Section 6.4 then shows summation: two such potentials give about 2 mV, three give about 3 mV, and the textbook calls temporal summation 'strictly a passive property of nerve cells'. The point-neuron abstraction is built on exactly this picture: the dendritic tree delivers current to one integration site with one threshold and one output. That abstraction is not a mistake, and most models of cortical populations depend on it, but it is an idealisation, and the way it fails is specific and measurable.

The failure comes from voltage-dependent conductances distributed along the dendrites. Imagine a thin basal or oblique dendrite receiving a burst of synapses that are active together and close enough to interact. Glutamate released at those spines depolarises the membrane through AMPA receptors; the depolarisation relieves the magnesium block of nearby NMDA receptors, which then pass a regenerative inward current. The result is a local event that does not need the axon initial segment to participate: a dendritic spike, or in its longer form a dendritic plateau potential. Augusto and Gambino (Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience, 2019) review the mechanism and the in vivo evidence, and make a point that changes how you should read the word threshold: the properties of an NMDA spike, including how many spines are needed, how long it lasts and how much dendrite it occupies, depend on the baseline membrane potential, because a depolarised membrane needs less glutamate to unblock more NMDA receptors. Threshold is a state variable of the branch, not a constant of the cell.

Three quantities convert this into something testable.

Amplitude. Gao and colleagues (Journal of Neurophysiology, volume 125, pages 23 to 42; received 2019, published online 2020, issue dated 2021) used laser-spot voltage-sensitive dye imaging in rat cortical slices to measure the voltage waveforms produced by spatially restricted glutamate release on thin basal dendrites. Local dendritic potentials lasted 200 to 500 ms and propagated to the cell body, where they produced sustained depolarisations of 10 to 20 mV. Against the textbook unitary potential of about 1 mV, a local dendritic event is therefore 10 to 20 times larger at the soma, and it lasts 20 to 50 times longer than a 10 ms excitatory postsynaptic potential. A purely passive cable cannot produce that: one scaled input cannot generate a somatic signal an order of magnitude larger than that input's baseline effect.

Spread. Distance attenuates. The same review notes that distal synaptic events undergo considerable voltage attenuation as they travel along the dendrite, which limits their influence on the axon initial segment. The somatic consequence of a dendritic event is therefore a fraction of its local amplitude: if a branch event reached 30 mV locally and 10 to 20 mV at the soma, between one third and two thirds of the local signal would have been lost. That figure is a constructed illustration of the attenuation logic, not a measurement from the paper. Attenuation is why dendritic location matters, and why identical conductance changes at two sites can have different consequences for output.

Input geometry. Whether a dendritic spike occurs at all depends on how active inputs are arranged. Earlier in vitro and modelling work found that active synapses had to be clustered on one segment to drive an NMDA spike; later work showed that roughly 10 clustered spines, or roughly 20 inputs distributed sparsely along a longer dendrite, can be sufficient, so clustering helps but is not a prerequisite. Twenty distributed inputs instead of ten clustered ones is a doubling of the co-active synapses required, which is the kind of quantitative difference that separates a mechanism from a slogan.

Three qualifications keep the picture honest. First, distinguish measurement from model output: the model in Gao and colleagues reproduced the recorded waveforms and predicted the direction of change in somatic input resistance and membrane time constant during a plateau, but not the magnitude, so the agreement supports the qualitative mechanism without supporting a claim of quantitative completeness. Second, distinguish tissue from behaving animal: most of the biophysics comes from slices, and although in vivo work reviewed by Augusto and Gambino links dendritic events to perception and behaviour in rodents, a correlation between dendritic events and behaviour is not by itself causal; establishing causality requires selective perturbation, which is the subject of lesson 76. Third, separate argued frameworks from results: Marvan, Polak, Bachmann and Phillips (Neuroscience of Consciousness, 2021) argue that apical amplification, the amplifying influence of inputs to the apical tuft of cortex, is a cellular mechanism of conscious perceptual experience. That paper presents a theoretical view and labels it as such, integrating three influential theories of consciousness rather than reporting a measurement of consciousness. Reading it as an established mechanism would repeat the reverse-inference error from lesson 29.
lessons.example:
Work one laboratory claim from the raw arithmetic upwards, showing at each step what would refute it. The claim is that a class of cortical pyramidal cells integrates inputs nonlinearly within single dendrites.

Step 1, establish the linear baseline. A unitary excitatory postsynaptic potential recorded at the soma of a spinal motor neuron is about 1 mV, and resting potential is about minus 65 mV with spike threshold in the region of minus 50 mV. Reaching threshold passively therefore requires about 15 exactly coincident unitary potentials, since 15 mV divided by 1 mV is 15. Because real inputs arrive with temporal dispersion and because membrane time constants and leak allow charge to decay between arrivals, the true number is larger; the figure of 15 is a lower bound obtained from the textbook numbers, and it should be reported as such rather than as a measurement of how many inputs a real cell needs.

Step 2, measure what one branch can do alone. With laser-spot glutamate release on a thin basal dendrite, the local response can last 200 to 500 ms and produce 10 to 20 mV of sustained depolarisation at the soma. Compare the two accounts. Under the passive account, one branch cannot deliver more than the sum of its individual inputs, so the somatic effect should stay in the low millivolts. Under the dendritic account, one active branch delivers a somatic depolarisation between 10 and 20 times the size of a unitary potential (10 divided by 1, and 20 divided by 1), sustained for 20 to 50 times longer than a 10 ms potential (200 divided by 10, and 500 divided by 10). The same measurement therefore discriminates between the accounts, which is what makes this a good experiment rather than a demonstration.

Step 3, write the predictions before the data. If the regenerative current depends on NMDA receptors, then blocking them should remove the supralinear component while leaving the linear sum of the AMPA-mediated responses intact; if the effect depends on inputs converging on one branch, then splitting the same number of stimulated spines across two distant branches should reduce the somatic depolarisation even though the total input is unchanged; and if attenuation is real, then moving the same conductance change from a distal to a proximal site should increase its somatic effect. Each prediction can fail, which is what gives the claim content.

Step 4, price the attenuation. Assume a branch event of 30 mV locally is recorded as 10 mV at the soma. That is a loss of two thirds of the signal (10 divided by 30 is 0.33, so 67 per cent is lost). If the same event were recorded as 20 mV at the soma, the loss would be one third. Any argument that dendritic events 'drive' spiking must therefore state where the electrode or indicator sits relative to the site of generation, because the amplitude difference between the two recording sites is larger than most of the effects being claimed.

Step 5, refuse to over-read the model. In the study at issue the compartmental model reproduced the voltage waveforms and correctly predicted the sign of the change in somatic input resistance and membrane time constant, but not the size of that change. A model whose qualitative predictions hold and whose quantitative predictions do not is useful precisely because it localises the missing piece, and it cannot be cited as a finished account.
lessons.question: A lab reports that stimulating a cluster of spines on one dendritic branch produces a 12 mV somatic depolarisation lasting 300 ms, and concludes that the cell is a point summing device. Which response is best?
lessons.answer: The result contradicts the point-summing account rather than supporting it, because a single branch produced a somatic depolarisation an order of magnitude larger than a unitary synaptic potential and lasting hundreds of milliseconds, which linear passive summation of individual inputs cannot generate.
lessons.distractor: The result supports the point-summing account because the cell still produced a normal action potential output, showing that the dendrite only delivers current to the soma.
lessons.correction: Producing a spike at the output says nothing about how the inputs were combined on the way there, which is the whole question. The informative comparison is between one branch's somatic effect and the size of a unitary input: at about 1 mV per unitary potential in the textbook example, a 12 mV sustained depolarisation from a single branch is on the order of ten unitary inputs delivered at once and held for hundreds of milliseconds. Passive summation of individually weak inputs cannot manufacture that amplitude from one site, which is why the finding is evidence of a local regenerative mechanism rather than of passive delivery. Note also the second half of the error: even if the cell were a point neuron, that would be a claim about a model, and the model would still need to reproduce the amplitude, the duration and the voltage dependence of the event. The defensible conclusion distinguishes what was measured (a large, long somatic depolarisation evoked by a restricted dendritic input) from what is inferred (an NMDA-receptor-dependent local regenerative current), and it names the experiment that would separate them, namely blocking the NMDA conductance and showing that the supralinear component disappears while the linear component survives.

depth.definitions: Terms you need before going further. A dendrite is the branched receiving structure of a neuron; a spine is a small protrusion that carries most excitatory synapses on pyramidal cells. An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is the transient depolarisation produced by one synaptic event; a unitary EPSP is the response to a single presynaptic action potential at one connection. Spatial and temporal summation are the passive addition of EPSPs arriving at different sites or different times, and cable theory is the framework that predicts how voltage spreads and decays along a passive dendrite, giving an attenuation factor between two locations. A compartmental model approximates a neuron as a set of connected electrical compartments, in contrast to the point neuron, which has no spatial extent. A dendritic spike is a regenerative depolarisation generated locally in a dendrite rather than at the axon initial segment. An NMDA spike is one driven by the voltage-dependent relief of magnesium block of NMDA receptors; a plateau potential is the longer-lasting form of the same class of event. Two-photon glutamate uncaging releases glutamate at chosen points with light, which is how specific spines are stimulated; voltage-sensitive dye imaging reports membrane voltage optically, which is how local dendritic waveforms were recorded in the study discussed here. Supralinear summation means the response to two inputs exceeds the sum of the responses to each alone. Prerequisites: lessons 21 and 25 (synaptic integration; NMDA-dependent potentiation) and lesson 29 (reverse inference).
depth.mechanism:
The mechanism has four steps and one feedback loop. Step one is glutamate binding: synaptic release activates AMPA receptors, which pass sodium and depolarise the local membrane. Step two is voltage-dependent relief of block: at resting potential the NMDA receptor channel is blocked by magnesium, and depolarisation expels the ion, so the receptor becomes able to pass current. Step three is regeneration: the resulting inward current depolarises the membrane further, which removes more block, which adds more current. That positive feedback is what makes the event local and self-sustaining rather than a passive decay, and it is why the size of the response depends on how many receptors can be recruited within a short distance and time window. Step four is termination and spread: the event decays, and its somatic footprint is set by how much of the local voltage survives propagation along the dendrite.

The loop that connects this to learning is that the same depolarisation promotes plasticity. Because the NMDA receptor is also the calcium entry route implicated in long-term potentiation, a dendritic event that strengthens co-active inputs is a plausible substrate for branch-level learning: inputs that arrive together on one branch are, in effect, tagged together. This is the point at which the dendritic story changes the interpretation of population recordings. If a cell's output depends on which inputs share a branch, then two stimuli that activate the same total number of afferents can produce different outputs, and an analysis that treats a neuron as a scalar firing rate will miss the variable that actually determines the response.

Limits matter as much as the mechanism. Much of the direct evidence comes from reduced preparations with pharmacological control, where the membrane state of the animal and the intact network are absent; the in vivo literature establishes that dendritic events occur and correlate with behaviour, not that they are necessary for it. The NMDA-spike threshold moves with membrane potential, so any claim that a particular number of spines is required is conditional on the depolarisation state, which in a behaving animal is set by ongoing network activity that the experimenter does not control. Finally, the receptor machinery is not exclusive to dendrites, so a pharmacological manipulation that abolishes a dendritic event may also act at the soma or on presynaptic terminals; attributing a behavioural effect to the dendritic event alone requires local manipulation, which is one reason the tools in lesson 76 matter.
depth.secondExample:
Contrast two papers that use the same vocabulary of dendritic computation but stand on different evidential footings.

In the first, Ujfalussy, Makara, Branco and Lengyel (eLife, 2015) worked from theory to data. They derived, from the statistics of presynaptic activity, the dendritic nonlinearity that would be optimal for integrating inputs efficiently in a circuit performing analogue computations with spiking neurons, and the derived form depended on presynaptic firing rates, membrane potential fluctuations and correlations. They then tested the prediction against two-photon glutamate uncaging responses in two types of cortical pyramidal cell. The order matters: a theory that specifies the shape of the nonlinearity in advance and then predicts responses to patterned stimulation is exposed to refutation in a way that a descriptive model fitted to the same data is not. When the predictions held, the result supported a functional link between cellular properties and circuit-level properties, which is a stronger claim than 'these cells are nonlinear'.

In the second, Marvan and colleagues (Neuroscience of Consciousness, 2021) argue that apical amplification is a cellular mechanism of conscious perception. The argument is integrative and theoretical: it shows how one cellular phenomenon could connect recurrent processing theory, global workspace broadcasting and integrated information theory. Its evidential footing is different in kind. Nothing in the paper measures consciousness, and the reader cannot fail to notice that the same cellular phenomenon is being asked to serve three theories that disagree with each other. That does not make the paper worthless; it makes it a hypothesis generator.

The transferable rule is to ask what each paper would look like if it were wrong. The eLife study would have failed if the derived nonlinearity had not matched the uncaging data in the predicted cell types. The consciousness paper would survive almost any cellular result, because it is a proposal about how a mechanism could fit into existing theories, and its central term is not operationalised in the experiment. When you meet dendritic vocabulary in a press release, sort the source this way before judging the claim.
depth.mistake:
A common and consequential misconception is that because a single neuron's firing rate is a coarse summary, single-neuron data are uninformative noise, so the only meaningful level of analysis is the population. The correction is that the abstraction and the mechanism are different objects. A rate code can be the right model for a question about decoding while the integrative mechanism inside the cell is nonlinear; the two statements are not in conflict, and pretending that they are leads researchers to design experiments whose stimuli cannot distinguish branch-specific from cell-wide integration. The diagnostic is to ask what the experiment would have to vary: if rearranging inputs across branches without changing their number changes the output, the rate summary is missing something.

A second misconception is the identification of dendritic spikes with memory. Because NMDA receptors mediate both regenerative dendritic events and forms of synaptic potentiation, it is tempting to say that the plateau potential is the memory and its location is the engram. The error is an inference from shared machinery to identity of function: the same receptor can support a fast electrical event and a slower biochemical one, and an event that strengthens co-active inputs is a mechanism that could contribute to storage without being storage. The diagnostic question is whether blocking the electrical event, without blocking the plasticity machinery, changes later behaviour; if the answer is unknown, the identity claim is not supported.

A third misconception treats the plateau as a digital all-or-none unit. In the recorded data the amplitude, duration and spatial extent vary with baseline potential and with the number and arrangement of active spines, so modelling the event as a binary switch discards the variables that carry the information.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are handed a one-paragraph claim: 'Cells in area X sum their inputs linearly, so their firing rate reports the total drive they receive.' Write a five-item study plan that could refute the claim, then compare against the model response.

Model response. First, measure the unitary somatic EPSP for a defined input class so the linear baseline is quantified rather than assumed. Second, use spatially restricted stimulation, such as two-photon glutamate uncaging or a patterned optogenetic stimulus with a small spot, on one branch versus on several branches while holding the total number of stimulated sites constant. Third, record voltage at the soma and, if possible, locally in the dendrite, and report the attenuation between the two sites, because amplitude comparisons are meaningless without stating where the measurement was made. Fourth, add a pharmacological test of the suspected regenerative conductance, with a control manipulation at the soma so that a global effect cannot be mistaken for a dendritic one. Fifth, pre-specify the analysis: state in advance what pattern of results would count as linear (somatic response proportional to the number of active inputs regardless of their arrangement), what would count as nonlinear but cell-wide (supralinearity independent of arrangement), and what would count as branch-specific (arrangement-dependent supralinearity). Self-review rubric, four criteria: (1) does the plan state a measurement of the linear baseline, not an assumption; (2) does it vary input geometry while holding input number constant; (3) does it identify the recording site and the attenuation between sites; (4) does it state a result that would falsify the linear claim. Score one point per criterion met; a plan that scores below three should be revised before any animal is used.
depth.summary: The lesson in one paragraph: a neuron is a spatially extended computing device whose dendrites contain voltage-dependent conductances, so summation can be nonlinear, threshold can be a state variable, and input arrangement can matter as much as input number. The evidence supporting this is layered, and the layers have different strengths: direct voltage measurements in slices establish the amplitude and duration of dendritic events; first-principles models that predict responses in advance establish the functional argument; in vivo recordings establish that the events occur in behaving animals and track behaviour; and theoretical frameworks that assign consciousness or memory to a cellular phenomenon are arguments rather than measurements. Transfer: when you next encounter a claim about a brain region, ask where in the cell the measurement was made, what the cell's output would look like if the dendritic mechanism were absent, and which manipulation would separate the two. That habit is what lets you read population-level results, spike-sorting quality metrics in lesson 77, and causal tool results in lesson 76 without accepting more than the data support.

visual.title: From one mV of summation to a regenerative branch event
visual.description: A two-column comparison diagram. The left column is the passive point-neuron account from the textbook; the right column is the dendritic account. A central scale bar gives amplitude in millivolts and a second bar gives duration in milliseconds so that the two columns can be compared numerically rather than metaphorically.
steps: Step 1 BASELINE (left column): one presynaptic action potential gives about 1 mV at the soma of a spinal motor neuron; three inputs summate to about 3 mV; a note attached to the column reads PASSIVE, NO SPATIAL STRUCTURE.

Step 2 SITE (right column): a pyramidal cell drawn with a soma, a thick apical trunk and thin basal branches; ten spines on one basal branch are marked as active together and the soma is marked as the recording site.

Step 3 LOCAL EVENT: at the active branch, label the sequence AMPA depolarisation, magnesium block relieved, NMDA inward current, regenerative local depolarisation; add the caption THRESHOLD DEPENDS ON BASELINE POTENTIAL.

Step 4 AMPLITUDE AND DURATION BARS: two horizontal bars under the right column, one labelled 10-20 mV at the soma and one labelled 200-500 ms; beside them, comparison bars for a 1 mV unitary potential and a 10 ms EPSP, with the ratios 10x to 20x and 20x to 50x printed next to the bars.

Step 5 ATTENUATION: an arrow from the active branch to the soma labelled WITH ATTENUATION, with a constructed illustration reading 30 mV locally and 10-20 mV at the soma, that is one third to two thirds of the signal lost, and a warning box stating that the recording site must always be stated.

Step 6 GEOMETRY: two insets side by side, one with ten spines on one branch and one with the same spines spread across two branches, captioned CLUSTERED vs DISTRIBUTED with the note that roughly 10 clustered versus roughly 20 distributed inputs are reported as sufficient in the reviewed literature.

Step 7 EVIDENCE TAGS: three labelled tags hanging off the diagram, MEASURED for the slice voltage recordings and the amplitude and duration figures, MODELLED for the compartmental reconstruction that matched waveform shape but not the magnitude of the resistance and time-constant change, and ARGUED for the apical-amplification hypothesis about consciousness.

lessons.title: Astrocytes at the tripartite synapse: a real signal with a contested function
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to describe the astrocyte calcium signal and the tripartite synapse concept, explain why the strongest challenge to gliotransmission was a technical one, and specify what a study has to show before you accept that an astrocyte-derived substance changed a synapse.

Start with what is not in dispute. Astrocytes are abundant: Goenaga, Araque, Kofuji and Herrera Moro Chao note in the opening of their Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience review (2023) that glia are as numerous in the brain as neurons, and that although astrocytes are not electrically excitable in the way neurons are, they display a form of excitability through changes in intracellular calcium. Astrocytes contact synapses, carry transporters and receptors that sense transmitter, and respond to neural activity. The UTHealth textbook treatment of glia in earlier levels of this course gives you the same background: these cells are not passive packing material.

What the tripartite synapse concept adds is the claim that the relationship is reciprocal. In the standard version, synaptic release activates G-protein-coupled receptors on the astrocyte process, which raises intracellular calcium; the calcium elevation triggers the release of neuroactive substances, called gliotransmitters; those substances act on neuronal receptors, including presynaptic receptors and extrasynaptic NMDA receptors that generate slow inward currents, and thereby modulate transmission and plasticity. Noriega-Prieto and Araque (Neurochemical Research, 2021) lay out this sequence, together with a figure listing the steps, and stress heterogeneity: the tripartite synapse does not behave the same way in every region or at every synapse. Their review is also careful about the level of the claim, presenting the concept as a framework that organises evidence rather than as a settled mechanism.

The calcium signal itself is more interesting than the textbook cartoon. Goenaga and colleagues describe two spatial regimes. Global calcium elevations involve the soma and last seconds; microdomain events occur in the fine distal processes, do not propagate to the soma, and are more frequent and asynchronous than somatic events. Some events are intrinsic and occur without external synaptic input; others are evoked by transmitter. The choice of indicator changes what you can see. In a systematic comparison in awake mice, Ye, Haroon, Salinas and Paukert (PLoS One, 2017) compared GCaMP3 with GCaMP6f and reported that image series in wild-type mice showed a much larger distance from perfect correlation with GCaMP6f (0.21 plus or minus 0.02, 11 mice) than with GCaMP3 (0.09 plus or minus 0.01, nine mice, p below 0.001), interpreting this as greater sensitivity of GCaMP6f to fast calcium dynamics at small spatial scales. That means the deviation from perfect correlation was about 2.3 times larger with the newer indicator: the same brain, the same window, a different count of what counts as an event. Any comparison of event rates across laboratories is therefore only interpretable if the indicator, its version, the filtering and the definition of an event are stated.

The contested step is release. The most influential challenge was not a philosophical objection but a genetic one. Sloan and Barres, writing a preview in Neuron (2014), summarised work by Fujita and colleagues showing that the dnSNARE mouse line used to demonstrate astrocytic vesicular release had leaky transgene expression in neurons, because the GFAP promoter used to target astrocytes is active in some neurons; the suppression of cortical electroencephalographic power that had been attributed to astrocytes losing the ability to release gliotransmitters was reproduced by directly inhibiting neuronal exocytosis. Sloan and Barres report that a second, independent GFAP-driven mouse line had the same problem, and note that gliotransmission had been reported to affect synaptic transmission by 20 to 30 per cent, an effect size large enough that an equally large technical artifact would be indistinguishable from it. The consequence for the field is specific rather than general: the calcium signal in astrocytes is not in question, the modulation of some synapses by some astrocyte-derived substances is supported by other methods, and the strong form of the tripartite synapse, namely that astrocytes routinely release vesicular gliotransmitters that shape synaptic transmission, remains contested.

Summarise the evidential layering the way you would for a dendritic claim. Measured: astrocytes respond to neural activity with calcium changes; microdomain events exist and are frequent; astrocyte processes contact synapses. Supported by multiple methods with effect sizes that are usually modest: astrocyte-derived substances and transporters modulate some synapses and some behaviours, with the review by Noriega-Prieto and Araque describing a subset of the strongest cases. Contested: routine vesicular release as a general mechanism, because a widely used tool for demonstrating it was shown to be non-specific. The lesson is not that glia matter less; it is that a mechanistic claim is only as good as the specificity of the tool that established it, which is also the theme of lesson 76.
lessons.example:
Work through what the indicator comparison actually means numerically, then use it to price a claim.

The Ye and colleagues comparison reports a goodness-of-match statistic for two indicators applied to the same preparation. Smaller values mean better agreement with perfect correlation, which in this analysis corresponds to fewer detected deviations in the signal. GCaMP3 gave 0.09 plus or minus 0.01 across nine mice; GCaMP6f gave 0.21 plus or minus 0.02 across 11 mice. The ratio of the central values is 0.21 divided by 0.09, which is about 2.3, and the difference was reported as significant with p below 0.001. Read that as a measurement about instruments, not about brains: changing the calcium indicator by one generation changed the measured statistic by a factor of roughly two and a third in the same wild-type animals.

Now price a claim that a particular manipulation increases astrocyte microdomain event rate by 40 per cent. If the same effect had been measured with the older indicator, the low detection sensitivity implies that many small fast events would be missed; if measured with the newer indicator in a different laboratory that filters differently or defines an event by a different amplitude threshold, the event count can shift with the definition alone. A 40 per cent change is smaller than the 2.3-fold shift the instrument produced, so the claim cannot be evaluated without those methodological details. The correct handling is not to discard the claim but to require within-study comparisons: the same indicator, the same processing pipeline, and a within-animal design in which each animal serves as its own control for the manipulation. Then the indicator shift cancels rather than contaminating the comparison.

Apply the same pricing logic to the release claim. Suppose the reported effect of blocking astrocytic vesicle release is a 20 to 30 per cent reduction in a synaptic measure, a range whose midpoint is 25 per cent. The Fujita and colleagues finding was that the genetic tool intended to block release in astrocytes also blocked exocytosis in neurons. A neuronal off-target effect of that size cannot be distinguished from an astrocyte-specific effect of that size in the same experiment, which is why the specificity of the tool, and not the size of the effect, was the crux of the dispute. The general rule: when the intended manipulation and its most plausible artifact predict the same direction and a similar magnitude, the experiment needs a design that separates them, such as cell-type-specific rescue, independent tool lines, or a pharmacological manipulation with a different mechanism of action.
lessons.question: A commentary argues that because the dnSNARE mouse line turned out to be non-specific, the whole idea that astrocytes modulate synapses should be abandoned. Which assessment fits the evidence?
lessons.answer: Too strong. The leak in that line undercuts the specific demonstration of vesicular gliotransmitter release in that model, but astrocyte calcium signalling, astrocyte-synapse contact, and modulation of some synapses by astrocyte-derived substances have support from other methods, so the affected claim is the strong vesicular-release version rather than the whole field.
lessons.distractor: A single non-specific tool invalidates every experiment that used related methods, so the tripartite synapse concept should be treated as disproved until entirely new techniques are available.
lessons.correction: The reasoning error is treating the failure of one instrument as a failure of a whole class of findings. The critique identified a specific defect: a promoter used for astrocyte targeting was also active in neurons, so a phenotype attributed to astrocyte release was reproducible by inhibiting neuronal exocytosis. That defect damages conclusions that depended on that line, and it should make you demand specificity evidence from any similar study, but it leaves intact results obtained by different routes, including direct calcium measurement, receptor manipulation on astrocyte processes, and pharmacological modulation whose site of action is verified. It is also worth noting what the critique did not do: it did not measure astrocyte release and find none; it showed that a particular experimental argument did not establish what it claimed. Statements in the literature should therefore be sorted by method rather than by field: the calcium observations, the contact anatomy, and the specific modulation results each get their own verdict. That sorting is exactly what the application task in this lesson asks you to practise.

depth.definitions: Key terms. An astrocyte is a star-shaped glial cell that contacts synapses, blood vessels and other glia; the tripartite synapse is the concept that a functional synapse includes the pre- and postsynaptic elements plus the surrounding astrocyte process. A gliotransmitter is a substance released by glia that acts on neuronal receptors; the term carries no commitment about the release route. Calcium microdomains are localised calcium elevations in fine astrocyte processes that do not spread to the soma; global events involve the soma and last longer. Genetically encoded calcium indicators (GECIs), of which the GCaMP family is the most used, report calcium via a fluorescent protein; the indicator version matters because sensitivity to fast, small events differs between versions. SNARE proteins mediate vesicle fusion, so a dominant-negative SNARE (dnSNARE) construct is used to block vesicular release; the GFAP promoter is a glial fibrillary acidic protein promoter frequently used to target astrocytes, and its cell-type specificity is the crux of the dispute discussed here. Slow inward currents are neuronal currents generated by extrasynaptic NMDA receptors and are used as a signature of gliotransmitter action. Effect size is the magnitude of a difference; an artifact of comparable size cannot be distinguished from a real effect of that size. Prerequisites: lesson 31 on release, and lesson 21 on synaptic integration.
depth.mechanism:
Take the proposed pathway one step at a time and ask at each step what has been shown. Synaptic activity releases transmitter, which reaches astrocyte processes, where metabotropic receptors and transporters produce a signal: this step is well established and is measurable as changes in astrocyte calcium and in membrane currents. Calcium rises, either globally or in a microdomain: also established, with the caveat that microdomain detection depends on the indicator and the optical resolution, as the GCaMP comparison shows. Calcium triggers release of a signalling molecule: this is where the route matters, because vesicular release through SNARE proteins, channel-mediated release, and transporter-mediated release have different pharmacological and genetic signatures, and the dnSNARE critique specifically removed confidence in the most-used evidence for the vesicular route. The released substance acts on neuronal receptors: supported for particular substances at particular synapses, and the signature used most often is a slow inward current through extrasynaptic NMDA receptors, which like all receptor-based signatures requires that the recording site and the receptor population be characterised.

Two structural features of the system make generalisation dangerous. First, astrocytes are heterogeneous, with regionally distinct gene expression and distinct calcium dynamics, so a mechanism demonstrated in one nucleus or one layer does not transfer automatically. Second, the spatial scale is small: an astrocyte process can contact thousands of synapses, so an effect on one synapse and an effect on a local pool of synapses are different claims with different tests, and a manipulation that changes the astrocyte globally cannot distinguish them. The limits follow directly: the mechanism is plausible and partially demonstrated, but the strength of any particular version depends on the specificity of the tool used, the spatial scale at which the manipulation acted, and whether the effect was demonstrated within a single preparation using a within-animal comparison.
depth.secondExample:
Take a different question from the same literature and watch the methodological lesson transfer: whether an astrocyte-derived signal modulates behaviour rather than a synapse.

A typical design selects a behaviour that depends on a circuit, manipulates an astrocyte signalling pathway, and reports a behavioural change. Suppose the manipulation is a calcium clamp or a metabotropic receptor knockout restricted to astrocytes, and the effect is a 30 per cent reduction in a conditioned response. Three questions decide how much the result supports the tripartite synapse. First, what is the temporal and spatial resolution of the manipulation? A genetic knockout removes the protein throughout development, so the behaviour may reflect a developmental consequence rather than an acute signalling function; the useful comparison is with an acute manipulation in the adult, whose effect can be timed and localised. Second, what is the control for the circuit-level consequence that does not involve gliotransmission at all? Manipulating astrocytes can change extracellular potassium, glutamate uptake, blood flow and metabolic supply, so a behavioural change is consistent with several mechanisms; ruling them out requires measurements of each, or at least a discussion that names them. Third, what is the specificity evidence for the targeting, given that the promoter-specificity problem was the crux of the earlier dispute?

Contrast that with the strongest available design in this literature, in which the release machinery, the receptor on the neuronal side, and the synaptic consequence are all manipulated independently, with a within-animal comparison and a measured effect size that exceeds the artifacts. The contrast is instructive: the second design does not merely add more evidence to the same argument, it closes off the alternatives that the first leaves open. Whenever you read a glia-and-cognition headline, ask which of these three questions the study answered, and note that 'astrocytes were manipulated and behaviour changed' answers none of them by itself.
depth.mistake:
The commonest error in this area is treating a calcium elevation as though it were a measured release event. Calcium imaging reports calcium; the inference that calcium caused release of a particular gliotransmitter which acted on a particular receptor is three separate steps, each of which can fail, and microdomain calcium events occur spontaneously in the absence of any synaptic input, so even the direction of causation is not guaranteed. The diagnostic question is: what would the calcium signal look like if no gliotransmitter were released? If the experiment cannot answer that, the calcium data do not test release.

A second error is the reverse, dismissing glia because one genetic tool proved leaky. Dismissing the whole literature discards results collected by different methods and, more importantly, discards the possibility that some synapses depend on astrocyte signalling and others do not. The diagnostic for this error is to ask which method established each specific claim, and to accept or reject the claim at that level.

A third error concerns interpretation of effect sizes. Gliotransmission has been reported to modulate synaptic transmission by 20 to 30 per cent, and artefacts of the tools involved are of the same order. A reader who accepts a 25 per cent modulation without checking tool specificity is accepting a claim whose magnitude is below the resolution of the method used to make it. The habit worth building is to ask, for every manipulation, what the largest plausible confound would do to the measurement, and whether the reported effect is distinguishable from it.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. A press summary states: 'Astrocytes release glutamate that sharpens memory, new study shows.' Write a four-question audit of the underlying study and a one-paragraph verdict, then compare with the model response.

Model response. Question one, targeting: which promoter or Cre line restricted the manipulation to astrocytes, and was leak into neurons tested, for example by co-labeling the transgene with a neuronal marker and quantifying the overlap? Question two, the measured variable: does the study measure release directly, or does it measure a downstream consequence such as a slow inward current or a behavioural score, and if the latter, which alternative mechanisms could produce the same consequence? Question three, specificity of the effect: is there an independent manipulation on the neuronal side, such as a receptor knockout in the target cells, that is required for the phenotype, and was a rescue attempted? Question four, arithmetic: what is the size of the reported effect, and is it larger than the plausible artifacts of the method, including the indicator's sensitivity if calcium imaging is used and the size of any non-specific effect of the manipulation? Verdict paragraph shape: name what the study establishes, at the level of the method that established it; state which step of the tripartite synapse hypothesis the result bears on; and state the one experiment that would most change your confidence. Self-review rubric, four criteria: (1) the audit names the targeting tool and its specificity test; (2) it distinguishes a measured release from an inferred one; (3) it requires an independent manipulation on the neuronal side; (4) it compares the effect size to the method's resolution. One point per criterion; a response that asserts that astrocytes 'are now known to' modulate memory without naming a method scores zero even if the study exists.
depth.summary: Synthesis: the astrocyte is a signalling cell whose calcium dynamics are real, spatially compartmentalised and indicator-dependent; the tripartite synapse is a framework that organises a heterogeneous set of findings; and the strong claim that astrocytes routinely release vesicular gliotransmitters that shape synaptic transmission rests on tools whose specificity was successfully challenged. Transfer the method: for any manipulation, ask what the largest plausible artifact would look like, then check whether the reported effect can be distinguished from it, and prefer within-preparation comparisons that cancel instrument differences. The same discipline, applied to optogenetic and chemogenetic tools, is the content of lesson 76, and applied to spike sorting it reappears in lesson 77.

lessons.title: Perineuronal nets and the extracellular matrix: what actually brakes plasticity
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to describe what a perineuronal net is made of, explain how it constrains plasticity, evaluate the digestion experiments that are used to demonstrate the constraint, and state why 'the critical period is closed' is an incomplete description.

Lesson 63 established that plasticity has windows and that the boundary between sensitive and insensitive periods is a measurement decision as much as a biological one. This lesson is about the physical structure that contributes to those boundaries.

A perineuronal net (PNN) is a specialised lattice of extracellular matrix that condenses around certain neurons during development and persists into adulthood. Sorg and colleagues, writing a review in the Journal of Neuroscience (2016), describe PNNs as unique extracellular matrix structures that wrap around particular neurons and control plasticity in the adult central nervous system, and they identify the major molecular players: hyaluronan, link proteins, tenascin-R, and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) of the lectican family, which includes aggrecan, versican, neurocan and brevican. The association with parvalbumin-containing fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons is the common case, but PNNs also surround some glutamatergic neurons, so 'PNNs mark inhibitory cells' is a tendency rather than a rule. Auer and colleagues, in a 2025 review in Cells, emphasise the same anatomy and add that PNNs regulate both plasticity and neuronal excitability, partly by their influence on parvalbumin interneuron physiology.

How does a net made of sugar chains brake plasticity? Three routes are described in the literature. The net physically restricts the rearrangement of connections by occupying the space around the synapse and by binding molecules that limit structural change. It biases the excitatory and inhibitory balance locally, because the fast-spiking interneurons that most often carry PNNs exert strong perisomatic inhibition and their excitability is modulated by the matrix around them. And it interacts with the molecular machinery of plasticity, so removing it changes the conditions under which synapses can be modified. Notice that these are not competing explanations; they are a division of labour, and the relative weight of each depends on the circuit.

The evidence pattern is a familiar one from this course. Correlational evidence shows that PNN intensity and coverage change with development, with learning, with ageing and in some disease models. Causal evidence comes from digestion: chondroitinase ABC (Ch-ABC) cleaves CSPG sugar chains and has been used to reactivate plasticity in adult animals, and the Sorg review and the Auer review both treat the digestion literature as the central experimental support for the brake hypothesis. There is an important limitation inside that tool. Ch-ABC removes all chondroitin sulfate chains regardless of their sulfation pattern, and the Sorg review notes that differences in sulfation pattern matter for plasticity, so a digestion experiment does not distinguish which CS species was doing the work. Genetic evidence is thinner than a reader might expect: Sorg and colleagues state that mice deficient in versican, neurocan or brevican have largely normal PNNs, whereas aggrecan-deficient cortical neurons are not stained by Wisteria floribunda agglutinin, a broad PNN marker. In other words, three of the four major lecticans tested were dispensable for the formation of a WFA-stainable net, while aggrecan was not, which is 75 per cent of the tested lecticans. That matters when a paper attributes a plasticity effect to 'the PNN' as a unitary object.

The human evidence about how graded the brake is comes from the visual system. Min's 2025 mini-review in Eye and Brain describes short-term monocular deprivation lasting a few hours in one day, which produces small and reversible changes in ocular dominance in adult humans, in favour of the previously deprived eye, whereas long-term deprivation over days, months or years produces profound and lasting effects. The review frames this as roughly 15 years of evidence that adult human visual cortex retains a limited capacity for deprivation-driven change, and discusses the research question of whether such short-term deprivation could be useful in amblyopia, where conventional patching of the better eye for 40 to 50 per cent of waking hours over several months loses effectiveness steeply after about 10 years of age.

Now the arithmetic that makes the boundary claim precise. Patching at 40 to 50 per cent of an assumed 16 waking hours is 6.4 to 8 hours per day; sustained over three months, about 91 days, that is 582 to 728 hours of deprivation. An acute short-term deprivation session of about three hours is therefore between about 194 and 243 times smaller in total dose. Any claim of the form 'adult plasticity is absent' or 'adult plasticity is present' has to specify the dose, because the same system that shows a small reversible shift after three hours might show nothing after a three-hour visual task at threshold or something larger after three months. Dose, direction, reversibility and the measured outcome belong in the sentence, not in a footnote.
lessons.example:
Work an audit of a digestion study, with the arithmetic shown at each step.

Step 1, read the intervention. A study reports that infusing Ch-ABC into adult visual cortex reactivated ocular dominance plasticity in a rodent, measured as a shift in the responses of cortical cells after a period of monocular deprivation. Two claims are bundled: that the digestion removed a brake on plasticity, and that the brake is specifically the chondroitin sulfate component of PNNs.

Step 2, price the tool's specificity. Ch-ABC cleaves chondroitin sulfate chains irrespective of sulfation pattern. If two CS species have opposing effects on plasticity, as the sulfation literature suggests is possible, the net effect of digestion is a sum of opposing influences and the experiment cannot attribute the result to either. The audit conclusion is not that the experiment is worthless but that it supports the general proposition that CSPGs constrain plasticity, and not the specific proposition about which CSPG species.

Step 3, check the genetic cross-check. If the same effect depended on one lectican, deleting it should reproduce a version of the effect. The published pattern is that versican, neurocan and brevican knockouts have largely normal nets while aggrecan-deficient neurons fail to stain with the broad WFA marker. Three of four tested lecticans are therefore dispensable for the structural hallmark, which means 'the PNN' cannot be treated as one interchangeable material. Compute the fraction explicitly before writing the sentence: three out of four is 75 per cent.

Step 4, compare doses across species and preparations. The rodent digestion experiment typically pairs the manipulation with a period of deprivation. The human short-term deprivation literature reports small reversible shifts after a few hours. A conventional clinical patching schedule at 40 to 50 per cent of waking hours over three months totals 582 to 728 hours if 16 waking hours are assumed, which is about 194 to 243 times the dose of a three-hour session. Any comparative statement about species or ages therefore has to state the dose, because the measured effects differ by more than an order of magnitude across doses within the same species.

Step 5, formulate the verdict with a falsifier. Verdict: CSPG digestion in adult cortex can restore a measurable, limited form of experience-dependent change, which supports a brake-like role for the matrix; the species of CSPG responsible and the extent to which the same mechanism limits human plasticity remain unknown. Falsifier: a well-powered study using a lectican-specific manipulation that fails to change the plasticity measure, or a digestion study in a preparation where matrix removal demonstrably leaves synaptic organisation untouched yet plasticity remains blocked, would each count against the brake interpretation.
lessons.question: A summary states that perineuronal nets close the critical period, so plasticity is impossible in the adult cortex. Which correction is best?
lessons.answer: PNNs are one contributor to the decline of plasticity rather than an on-off switch: digestion experiments show a brake-like role for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, adult humans show small reversible ocular dominance shifts after a few hours of monocular deprivation, and the effect depends on the dose and the measured outcome.
lessons.distractor: PNNs cannot influence plasticity at all, because deleting three of the four major lecticans leaves the net structure intact in mice.
lessons.correction: The second statement over-corrects on the basis of the wrong evidence. Gene knockouts and enzymatic digestion test different things: knockouts remove one component and the remaining components can still assemble a WFA-stainable structure, whereas digestion removes the chondroitin sulfate chains themselves, and it is the digestion experiments that supply the positive causal evidence. The finding that three of four lectican knockouts have largely normal nets limits what can be attributed to those individual proteins; it does not show that the matrix is inert. The better statement keeps three qualifications visible: the mechanism is graded rather than binary, as the small and reversible adult shifts after a few hours of deprivation show; the burden is dose-dependent, since a clinical-scale patching schedule accumulates hundreds of hours while laboratory short-term deprivation accumulates a few; and the causal tool has a known specificity limitation, because Ch-ABC removes all chondroitin sulfate chains regardless of sulfation. A reader who keeps those three qualifications in the sentence has a claim that survives contact with the literature.

depth.definitions: Terms. The extracellular matrix is the material between cells, and in the central nervous system it is organised into lattices, of which the perineuronal net is the best characterised. Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) are matrix molecules whose protein core carries chondroitin sulfate sugar chains; the lectican family includes aggrecan, versican, neurocan and brevican. Sulfation pattern means the placement of sulfate groups along the sugar chain, which changes the molecule's binding partners and its effect on plasticity. Hyaluronan is a long sugar polymer that forms the backbone of the net, and tenascin-R is a linker molecule in the same structure. Wisteria floribunda agglutinin (WFA) is a plant lectin used as a broad histological marker for PNNs, so 'WFA-stainable' is an operational definition of a net rather than a complete description of matrix composition. Chondroitinase ABC (Ch-ABC) is an enzyme that cleaves chondroitin sulfate chains; because it does not discriminate between sulfation patterns, it is a broad rather than a selective tool. Parvalbumin interneurons are fast-spiking inhibitory cells that often carry PNNs and provide perisomatic inhibition. Ocular dominance is the relative influence of the two eyes on a cortical neuron, and monocular deprivation is the experimental closure or blurring of one eye. Prerequisites: lessons 42 and 63 on experience-dependent wiring and critical periods.
depth.mechanism:
The mechanism connects three levels: the molecular composition of the matrix, the physiology of the cells it wraps, and the plasticity of the synapses in their neighbourhood. At the molecular level, hyaluronan, link proteins, tenascins and CSPGs assemble into a lattice held together by multiple, partly redundant interactions. That redundancy explains why single-gene deletions often leave a stainable structure: the assembly does not depend on any one lectican except aggrecan, whose loss prevents WFA staining of cortical primary neurons, suggesting a structurally central role. The practical consequence is that genetic manipulations of this system are usually partial, and their negative results have low power against the hypothesis unless the residual structure is quantified.

At the cellular level, the cells most often wrapped are fast-spiking parvalbumin interneurons, which control the timing of inhibition onto the perisomatic region of pyramidal cells. The matrix around them modulates their excitability and the geometry of their synaptic input, and the 2025 review by Auer and colleagues describes electrophysiological differences in the cells that carry nets. Because perisomatic inhibition gates the window during which excitatory inputs can drive plasticity, a change in interneuron excitability is a plausible route by which a non-neuronal structure changes a synaptic rule. This is a chain of inference with several links, and each link has been measured in some preparations and inferred in others; the fair statement is that the circuit-level route is supported but not fully specified.

At the synaptic level, matrix removal is followed by renewed structural and functional rearrangement, which is what the digestion literature shows. Note the logical structure of that evidence: the manipulation is enzymatic and reversible in principle, the outcome is measured on a plasticity assay, and the interpretation depends on the assumption that digestion did not damage tissue in unrelated ways. That assumption deserves explicit testing, because an enzyme infusion is not a clean perturbation, and a lesion that happens to increase excitability could produce a plasticity-like result without removing a brake. The limits are therefore mirrored in the recommendations: quantify residual matrix after genetic manipulation, test for damage after enzymatic manipulation, specify the sulfation species when claiming a molecular target, and state the dose of the experience that the plasticity assay delivered.
depth.secondExample:
Apply the same reasoning to a second context where PNNs are invoked: memory persistence after learning. A study trains animals on a memory task, then digests matrix in a relevant region and reports that a normally persistent memory becomes vulnerable to disruption, or that a normally transient memory becomes durable. The interpretation offered is that the net stabilises the trace by restricting structural reorganisation.

Three checks decide how much the study supports that interpretation, and they are the same three checks from the previous context. First, specificity: which component was removed and with what tool, and does the result survive a manipulation with a different mechanism, such as a lectican-specific genetic tool or a sulfation-selective enzyme? Second, damage and side effects: was matrix removal quantified, and was there an independent measure showing that the region's basic physiology was intact, for example input-output curves and baseline firing? Third, the boundary conditions of the behavioural claim: was the memory tested with the same cue and the same response at the same delay, and was the comparison against an appropriate control that received the infusion without the behavioural training? A result that survives all three is a strong claim about matrix-dependent memory persistence; a result that survives only the first is a report that an enzyme changed a behaviour.

Now transfer the pattern one step further, to the developmental claim that nets close critical periods in the visual system. The strongest version asserts that a developmental increase in matrix coverage is necessary and sufficient for the end of the sensitive period. Testing necessity requires removing matrix during development without other changes; testing sufficiency requires adding or accelerating matrix formation and showing earlier closure. The published literature contains partial versions of both, mainly in rodents, which is why the honest formulation is that matrix maturation is one of several contributors, alongside the maturation of inhibition, myelin-related signalling, and changes intrinsic to the neurons themselves. Notice how different the second formulation is in risk: it can be wrong in specific ways, which is the mark of a scientific claim.
depth.mistake:
A frequent error is to treat 'critical period' and 'brake' as a single switch, so that any evidence of adult plasticity is read as proof that the critical period is not closed, and any evidence of a brake is read as proof that adults cannot learn. Both readings collapse a graded system into a binary. The diagnostic questions are: what was the dose of the experience, what was the outcome measure, and how large was the change relative to measurement noise? The adult monocular deprivation literature is instructive precisely because its effects are described as small and reversible, which is incompatible with the binary reading in either direction.

A second error is to treat all PNN components as interchangeable because they are all 'the matrix'. The knockout pattern gives the counterexample: three of four tested lecticans are dispensable for the structural marker while aggrecan is not, and digestion destroys all chondroitin sulfate chains irrespective of sulfation. A paper that attributes a plasticity effect to 'perineuronal nets' as a single substance is therefore making a weaker claim than it appears to, and the correction is to state which molecule was manipulated by which tool.

A third error is a clinical one that this course must name explicitly: because amblyopia treatment and short-term deprivation research appear in the same literature, a reader may conclude that a lesson about visual plasticity constitutes advice about treatment. It does not. Treatment decisions for a visual disorder belong with an ophthalmologist or orthoptist, and the research questions reviewed in the cited sources are research questions about plasticity, not protocols to be self-administered.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are reviewing a preprint that reports: 'Digesting perineuronal nets in adult mouse auditory cortex restores juvenile-like plasticity; therefore the critical period is caused by the extracellular matrix.' Write a five-line review, each line making one specific demand, then compare with the model response.

Model response. Line one, tool specificity: state that chondroitinase ABC cleaves all chondroitin sulfate chains regardless of sulfation, and require either a sulfation-selective manipulation or a qualification of the molecular claim. Line two, residual matrix: require quantification of matrix staining after the treatment, plus a marker for damage, so that the effect can be attributed to matrix loss rather than to a general lesion. Line three, dose and outcome: require the deprivation or training dose in hours and the outcome measure with its effect size and variability, so that 'juvenile-like' becomes a quantity. Line four, controls: require a comparison manipulation that produces the same increase in excitability without removing matrix, because a preparation that is simply more excitable may pass a plasticity assay for the wrong reason. Line five, causal wording: require the conclusion to be rewritten from 'caused by' to something the design can support, such as 'depends on the chondroitin sulfate component of the matrix in this preparation'. Self-review rubric, five criteria: (1) names the tool and its specificity limit; (2) demands a damage or excitability control; (3) demands a dose and an effect size; (4) demands residual-matrix quantification; (5) rewrites the causal claim into one the design can bear. One point per criterion.
depth.summary: Synthesis: plasticity declines are not caused by one structure, and the perineuronal net is best understood as a component of a braking system that also includes the maturation of inhibition and other molecular changes. The causal evidence for the matrix component comes mainly from enzymatic digestion, which is strong on the general proposition and weak on the molecular identity of the target, while genetic evidence shows structural redundancy. Human evidence for the gradation of the brake comes from short-term deprivation effects that are small, reversible and dose-dependent. Transfer: whenever you read that a window has closed, ask for the dose of experience delivered, the outcome measure, the specificity of the tool, and the control that shows the manipulation did not simply make the tissue more excitable. Those four questions generalise to any claim about a brake on plasticity, including claims about learning apps and about ageing.
