Falsifier box: a final panel listing the observations that would count against the brake account, namely a lectican-specific manipulation with no effect on the plasticity measure, or matrix removal that leaves tissue physiology intact yet fails to change plasticity.

lessons.title: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis: how two strong studies reached opposite answers
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to state the two positions in the dispute over new neurons in the adult human hippocampus, identify the specific methodological choices that generate the disagreement, compute how far apart the published estimates are, and describe what kind of evidence would settle the question.

The question is narrow and testable: does the adult human dentate gyrus recruit new neurons? It has two answers in the primary literature, both published in 2018, both in high-visibility journals, and both based on human tissue.

The negative case. Sorrells and colleagues, in Nature (2018), examined 59 postmortem and intraoperative samples of human hippocampus spanning fetal life to adulthood, together with monkey tissue. They report a defined population of progenitor cells that does not coalesce in the subgranular zone during human fetal or postnatal development, a sharp decline in proliferating progenitors and young neurons in the first year of life, only a few isolated young neurons by 7 and 13 years of age, and no young neurons detected in the dentate gyrus of adults aged 18 to 77 (17 postmortem and 12 epilepsy cases). The key quantities are in the cell counts: cells expressing doublecortin together with polysialylated neural cell adhesion molecule (DCX+PSA-NCAM+) in the granule cell layer numbered 1,618 per square millimetre at birth (standard deviation 780), 292.9 per square millimetre at one year, and 12.4 per square millimetre by 7 years. Those are declines of about 82 per cent from birth to one year, about 96 per cent from one year to seven years, and about 99 per cent from birth to seven years, a change in the counted density by roughly a factor of 130. The authors conclude that adult human dentate gyrus neurogenesis does not continue, or is extremely rare.

The positive case. Boldrini and colleagues, in Cell Stem Cell in the same year, examined hippocampal tissue from 28 people aged 14 to 79 without neuropsychiatric disease, using immunohistochemistry and messenger RNA markers for cells at several maturational stages, and reported neural progenitors, immature neurons and mature granule neurons in the adult dentate gyrus, with preserved numbers of intermediate progenitors and immature neurons in older individuals but declines in quiescent progenitors, in measures of neural plasticity, and in angiogenesis.

Two further sources make the disagreement legible. Paredes and colleagues (Cell Stem Cell, 2018) reply directly to the positive report and describe the identification problem in concrete terms. In adult tissue, DCX staining appeared in small round cells not only in the granule cell layer but also in the hilus and in other regions including white matter, and many of those cells appeared to be non-neuronal glia. Some ramified DCX-positive cells with differentiated neuronal morphology were also observed. Their verdict is that stereological counting, which the positive study uses, is only informative if what is being counted is correctly identified, and they note that other laboratories reporting few adult DCX-positive cells (1 to 7 cells per square millimetre) showed examples that were either small round cells or large mature-looking neurons. Their own control for tissue preservation was direct rather than statistical: in two adult cases with a postmortem interval under five hours that were perfused with paraformaldehyde before brain removal, the pattern was unchanged, with young neurons and progenitors present in children and absent in adults, while in the same adult samples they detected young neurons in the ventricular wall and entorhinal cortex. If fixation or postmortem delay had destroyed the signal everywhere, those other regions should have been negative too, so preservation alone does not explain the absence in the dentate gyrus.

The methodological counter-case. Tartt and colleagues, in the companion letter, note that marker detection depends on tissue processing, fixation time, postmortem interval and other factors that affect antigen preservation and messenger RNA integrity, and that the positive study used a protocol for fresh frozen tissue with shorter fixation and without harsh antigen retrieval, which preserves messenger RNA better. They add a substantive distinction: in their sample, older individuals showed lower numbers of quiescent progenitors without lower numbers of intermediate progenitors or immature neurons, so ageing may reduce the reservoir rather than the output. They also list confounding information that human tissue studies often lack, including psychiatric diagnoses, medications and recent drug use.

Put the numbers side by side, using the figures as reported by the sources rather than as the labels people attach to them. A commentary summarising the carbon-14 birthdating work reports an estimate of about 700 new neurons added to the human hippocampus per day, with roughly one third of hippocampal neurons able to undergo replacement; the negative study detected no young neurons in adult dentate gyrus; the adult densities reported by other laboratories were 1 to 7 cells per square millimetre. Treating the 700-per-day figure as one anchor and 1 to 7 cells per square millimetre as the other, the two pictures differ by between two and nearly three orders of magnitude, and 700 divided by 7 is 100 while 700 divided by 1 is 700. Quantities that far apart are not a matter of emphasis. At least one set of measurements must be measuring something different, and the plausible candidates are the identity of the counted cells, the tissue processing, and the choice of marker.

The wider literature has not collapsed the disagreement. Alonso-Moreno, Gallardo-Caballero, Pradanos-Senen and Llorens-Martin, reviewing human adult hippocampal neurogenesis in health and disease in Aging Brain (2025), report continuing inconsistency, including conflicting results on vascular and astrocytic features of the neurogenic niche across laboratories and a debate over whether single-cell transcriptomic mapping reconciles or prolongs the controversy. Lima and Gomes-Leal, writing in Neural Regeneration Research (2019), summarise the history from Altman and Das in 1965 through Eriksson in 1998 and attribute the discrepancies largely to methodological differences such as tissue overfixation.

Three habits follow. First, in a dispute like this, compare methods before comparing conclusions, because the disagreement is usually located in a procedure rather than in an observation. Second, be suspicious of a term doing work it cannot do: young neuron is defined operationally by markers and morphology, and every disagreement about presence is at bottom a disagreement about identification. Third, keep the evidential status explicit: as of these sources the question is unresolved, with a well-argued negative case resting on direct counts and preservation controls, a well-argued positive case resting on marker-based counts in a different tissue protocol, and no consensus synthesis.
lessons.example:
Work an arithmetic and logic check on the two claims, then write the sentence you would put in a review.

Step 1, reproduce the negative study's own curve. DCX+PSA-NCAM+ density in the granule cell layer was 1,618 per square millimetre at birth with a standard deviation of 780, 292.9 at one year with a standard deviation of 142.8, and 12.4 at seven years with a standard deviation of 5.3. Birth to one year is a fall from 1,618 to 292.9, which is 1,325.1 cells per square millimetre lost, or about 82 per cent of the starting value. One year to seven years is a fall from 292.9 to 12.4, about 96 per cent of the one-year value. Over the whole span the density falls by about 99 per cent, a factor of 1,618 divided by 12.4, which is about 130. Two features of these numbers are worth noticing. First, the error bars are large relative to the means at the youngest ages, so a single sample at one year could plausibly be measured anywhere in a wide band. Second, the trend direction is not in doubt, because even the upper bound at seven years is far below the lower bound at birth.

Step 2, compare the anchors across studies. The birthdating estimate reported in the commentary is about 700 new neurons per day in the adult human hippocampus. The adult densities reported by the laboratories that do detect DCX-positive cells are 1 to 7 per square millimetre. Dividing 700 by 7 gives 100, and 700 by 1 gives 700. Even allowing for the fact that density per square millimetre and cells added per day are different units, the gap is two to three orders of magnitude, so both anchors cannot describe the same process at the same rate.

Step 3, identify the discriminating procedures. Three are decisive in this literature. Marker combination: DCX alone labels cells that may not be neuronal, whereas DCX together with PSA-NCAM, or together with a morphology criterion such as an elongated nucleus and a leading process, is more restrictive, and the reply letter reports that PSA-NCAM-positive cells in adult dentate gyrus were DCX-negative with large round nuclei and NeuN expression, which is the profile of mature neurons. Tissue protocol: fresh frozen tissue with short fixation and no harsh antigen retrieval preserves messenger RNA, while longer fixation and antigen retrieval can preserve protein immunoreactivity at the cost of RNA, so the two studies may be measuring complementary but non-identical signals. Sampling frame: surgical specimens from epilepsy surgery and autopsy cases from different sources differ in premortem state and delay, and the reply letter's strongest control was two adult cases with postmortem interval under five hours perfused before removal, in which adult dentate gyrus remained negative while other regions in the same tissue showed young neurons.

Step 4, write the review sentence. A defensible version reads: the two studies used tissue from different sources with different fixation protocols and different cell-identification criteria, and their estimates of adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis differ by two to three orders of magnitude, so the discrepancy cannot be resolved by averaging and must be addressed by pre-registered side-by-side processing of the same tissue with agreed identification criteria. Note what that sentence does: it states what would settle the question, which is more useful than taking a side.
lessons.question: A review asserts that the adult human hippocampus generates about 700 new neurons per day, so the negative 2018 study should be discounted. Which response is best?
lessons.answer: The two estimates differ by two to three orders of magnitude and come from different methods and tissue protocols, so neither can be used to dismiss the other; the honest position is that the identification criteria and tissue processing are the crux, and the dispute remains unresolved.
lessons.distractor: The negative study should be discounted because it counted cells with a single marker and used autopsy tissue, whereas the positive estimate used carbon-14 birthdating, which measures cell age directly and is therefore unaffected by fixation.
lessons.correction: The second answer contains a real point wrapped in an overstatement. Carbon-14 birthdating does measure something different from marker immunoreactivity, namely the date at which a cell's DNA was synthesised, and it is less vulnerable to antigen loss. But it depends on its own assumptions about the cell population being modelled, and the commentary that reports the 700-per-day figure explicitly notes that the study's results were not confirmed by the subsequent report. Meanwhile the negative study did not rest on a single marker or on autopsy tissue alone: it combined doublecortin with PSA-NCAM and other markers, used both postmortem and surgical samples, and in the reply letter reported two adult cases with postmortem interval under five hours in which the adult dentate gyrus remained negative while other regions of the same tissue contained young neurons. The correct move is therefore not to pick a winner but to name the discriminating procedure, which in this case is processing tissue from the same source through both protocols with pre-agreed identification criteria and quantification methods. A reader who can state that experiment has understood the dispute; a reader who cites one number as settled has not.

depth.definitions: Terms. The dentate gyrus is the hippocampal subfield that contains the granule cell layer and the subgranular zone where adult neurogenesis is claimed to occur. Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule-associated protein expressed in immature neurons, widely used as a young-neuron marker, and the subject of the identification dispute because it also labels cells of other types in adult human tissue. PSA-NCAM is polysialylated neural cell adhesion molecule, another immaturity-associated marker frequently combined with DCX. Ki-67 marks proliferating cells and SOX1 and SOX2 are progenitor-associated transcription factors. NeuN marks mature neuronal nuclei. Stereology is a set of sampling principles designed to obtain unbiased counts from sections, and its value depends on the identification of the objects counted. The postmortem interval is the delay between death and fixation, and fixation is the chemical preservation step; both affect the antigens and RNA that markers detect. Carbon-14 birthdating exploits the transient rise in atmospheric carbon-14 from nuclear tests to date the DNA of cells that divided while the signal was elevated. Prerequisites: lesson 26 on hippocampal models and lesson 65 on ageing measures.
depth.mechanism:
The biology itself is not the disputed part; the measurement is. In rodents, the subgranular zone contains radial glia-like cells that divide, produce intermediate progenitors, and give rise to immature neurons that migrate a short distance into the granule cell layer, extend dendrites, receive input and integrate into the circuit. The process is activity-sensitive: exercise and learning are reported to increase it and stress to decrease it. Nothing in this lesson challenges the rodent literature, which is why the human question is worth asking rather than dismissing.

The conflict arises at four measurement steps, each of which behaves differently in human tissue. First, sampling: human tissue comes from autopsy or from surgical resections performed to treat epilepsy, so the premortem state, the delay to fixation and the disease context vary and are often incompletely documented, and the positive study's authors note that missing information on psychiatric diagnosis and medication can matter because such factors affect the anterior dentate gyrus selectively. Second, preservation: fixation time and antigen retrieval trade protein immunoreactivity against RNA integrity, so a protocol optimised for one marker class may systematically undercount the other. Third, identification: in adults, cells that express young-neuron markers include small round cells in the hilus and in white matter that appear non-neuronal, so a marker-based count depends on the decision rule for what counts, and this is why the reply letter states that stereology helps only if the counted objects are correctly identified. Fourth, quantification: density per unit area, total counts from stereology, and rate estimates from birthdating are different quantities with different assumptions, and comparing them directly is not a like-for-like test.

The limits of the whole literature follow from these steps. No human study can manipulate the system, so all evidence is observational. Sample sizes are small by design because tissue is scarce. And because the strongest disagreements are procedural, the resolution is procedural too: side-by-side processing with shared criteria, agreement on identification, and pre-specified quantification. Until that exists, both a positive and a negative reading of the same question are defensible interpretations of different protocols.
depth.secondExample:
Transfer the structure of this dispute to a second field where the same pattern appears: estimating the number of a cell type in human post-mortem tissue, for example the density of a specific interneuron class in a cortical region.

The pattern repeats in three steps. First, the operational definition drives the number: if the marker is a calcium-binding protein that is also expressed at low levels in other cells, then the difference between studies may be a threshold decision rather than a biological difference, which is exactly the DCX situation. Second, tissue history drives the number: a study that collects with a long delay to fixation will report fewer detectable cells than a study with rapid perfusion, and the difference will be attributed to disease unless the delay is matched between groups. Third, quantification drives the comparison: counts per section, counts per volume with stereology, and optical density measures are not interchangeable, so a meta-analysis that pools them without conversion is pooling unlike quantities.

The contrast with a rodent experiment is instructive and it is not about prestige. In rodents the investigator controls genotype, environment, age and perfusion, can use genetic labelling rather than antibodies, and can add a manipulation. Those advantages are why the rodent literature is the one that settles mechanistic questions about neurogenesis and why the human literature is the one that settles questions about the human. A careful reader therefore uses the rodent work to understand the process, and the human work to answer the human question, while keeping the two verdicts separate.

A third application closes the loop with lesson 65: when a claim concerns change with age in human tissue, ask whether the comparison is cross-sectional or within-person, whether the tissue processing was matched across ages, and whether the effect size exceeds the variability introduced by processing. In ageing studies of scarce human tissue, processing differences between young and old cohorts are a standing hazard, and the discipline of naming them is the only protection available.
depth.mistake:
The characteristic error in this literature is to treat a marker as an identity. DCX is a protein expressed with a particular developmental profile in rodents, and it is convenient to read its presence in adult human tissue as the presence of a young neuron. The reply letter in this dispute documents why that inference fails: adult DCX signal appears in small round cells in the hilus and in white matter, many apparently glial, and PSA-NCAM-positive cells in adult dentate gyrus were DCX-negative with large round nuclei and NeuN expression, which is the profile of mature neurons. The diagnostic move is to require at least two independent identification criteria, such as a second immaturity marker plus morphology, and to state the criteria before counting.

The second error is the mirror image: treating a failed detection as proof of absence. Absence of a signal can be produced by absence of the cell, by loss of the antigen, by the wrong protocol, or by a count threshold that hides a rare object. The negative study anticipated this with an internal control, namely that in the same adult tissue young neurons were detected in the ventricular wall and entorhinal cortex while the dentate gyrus was negative, which is the kind of positive control that converts a negative result into evidence. A reader should demand exactly that kind of control before accepting any claim that something is absent.

The third error is choosing a side because a number sounds more impressive. The 700-per-day figure is memorable and large; the negative result is stark and equally memorable. Neither is a reason to stop reading. The arithmetic above shows the two pictures differ by two to three orders of magnitude, which is itself the finding, because it tells you where the disagreement lives.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are asked to draft a one-page protocol for a study intended to reduce the disagreement. Include the tissue sources, the identification criteria, the processing, the quantification and the pre-specified analysis. Then compare with the model response.

Model response. Tissue sources: obtain both surgical and autopsy material, record for every case the postmortem interval, the premortem diagnoses and medication history, and match the young and old groups on those variables rather than only on age. Identification: require two independent immaturity markers plus a morphology criterion, with electron microscopy on a subsample to characterise the counted cells, and define the criteria and the counting rules in the protocol before unblinding. Processing: split each case across both protocols, fresh frozen with short fixation and fixed material with standard antigen retrieval, so that protocol is a within-case factor rather than a between-study difference. Quantification: report density, total stereological estimate and any RNA-based measure separately, with pre-specified conversion assumptions if they are compared. Analysis: pre-register the primary outcome as the between-protocol difference in young-neuron counts, with a sample size justified for the smallest effect of interest, and state in advance what pattern would support each position. Self-review rubric, five criteria: (1) protocol is a within-case factor; (2) two or more identification criteria with a morphology check; (3) postmortem interval and medication history recorded and matched; (4) quantification methods reported separately with stated assumptions; (5) primary outcome pre-specified with a stated smallest effect of interest. A protocol that omits the within-case design cannot answer the question it was written to answer, however good the rest of it is.
depth.summary: Synthesis: the dispute over adult human hippocampal neurogenesis is not a dispute about whether cells divide, it is a dispute about what a marker detects in adult human tissue, how fixation and postmortem delay change what can be detected, and which quantification makes two studies comparable. The negative case rests on direct counts with internal positive controls; the positive case rests on marker-based counts under a different tissue protocol; the birthdating estimate sits on a third methodological footing; and the estimated rates differ by two to three orders of magnitude, which is the diagnostic signal that the disagreement is procedural. Transfer: for any presence-or-absence claim in human tissue, ask for the identification criteria, the processing controls and the internal positive control, and for any quantitative discrepancy, compute the ratio before adjudicating, because a factor of a hundred between studies tells you where to look and a factor of two might tell you nothing at all.

lessons.title: Microglia and synapse elimination: a mouse mechanism and a human extrapolation
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to describe how microglia eliminate synapses in the developing mouse visual pathway, state which parts of that account are supported by causal manipulations and which are hypotheses, and explain why the popular claim that microglia prune human adolescent synapses is an extrapolation rather than a measurement.

Two elimination stories exist in the literature, and they are not usually told side by side. The first is a textbook story about competition. The UTHealth chapter Synapse Formation, Survival, and Elimination, section 9.17, describes elimination at the neuromuscular junction as a reduction in the number of synaptic inputs accompanied by an increase in the complexity and strength of what remains, with activity-dependent competition favouring more active inputs, direct competition for trophic factors supplied by the target, and the possibility of a retrograde messenger provoking elimination. No immune cell is required for that account, and the mechanism is described as withdrawal of the presynaptic terminal with loss of acetylcholine receptors.

The second story adds microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system. Schafer and colleagues, in Neuron (2012), studied the retinogeniculate system of the mouse, where axons from the two eyes compete for territory in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus during the first postnatal week, with pruning largely complete by postnatal day 9 or 10. Using anterograde tracers to label retinal ganglion cell inputs from each eye, fluorescently labelled microglia, and the lysosomal marker CD68, they showed that microglia engulf presynaptic inputs during peak pruning, that engulfment is significantly increased at the peak, around postnatal day 5, relative to older ages, that engulfment is greater in synapse-enriched regions of the nucleus than in the non-synaptic optic tract, and that engulfment depends on neural activity and on the microglia phagocytic pathway complement receptor 3 and its ligand C3. Disrupting that pathway produced sustained deficits in synaptic connectivity, which is the causal step that makes this more than an observation of contact. Two features of the methods deserve attention: the per-age sample size was three mice in the quantification shown, and the engulfment analysis was strengthened by immuno-electron microscopy localising a vesicular glutamate transporter to retinal terminals and to microglia.

The mechanistic account has grown more complicated, and the complications are informative. Soteros and Sia, reviewing complement-dependent synapse elimination (WIREs Mechanisms of Disease, 2021), describe a regulated system rather than a one-way disposal route: complement proteins opsonise excess synapses and microglia bearing complement receptors phagocytose them, while complement inhibitors and signals controlling microglial recruitment modulate the process, and removing inhibitory factors such as CD47 or the complement inhibitor SRPX2 reduces synapse density, which implies that the system is held in check as well as driven. De Deus, Faborode and Nandi, reviewing the mouse genetic evidence (Developmental Neuroscience, 2024), organise the field by signal class, including eat-me, find-me and do-not-eat signals, and add two findings that limit any sweeping statement. First, pruning can be input-specific within one cell: GPR56-mediated, phosphatidylserine-dependent elimination in the hippocampus affected one dendritic domain that receives entorhinal input but not another that receives CA3 input. Second, removing one candidate signal need not change elimination: TWEAK-deficient mice showed no difference in phagocytosis of retinal ganglion cell terminals in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, indicating that this molecule is not required for the early phase of refinement.

Now the extrapolation, stated as arithmetic rather than as opinion. The mouse window in which this mechanism is demonstrated is a matter of days: pruning is largely complete by postnatal day 9 or 10. Human cortical and visual maturation proceeds over years. As a scaling illustration, ten days compared with a ten-year developmental span is a factor of about 365, so any transfer of the mouse timeline to a human one requires an explicit argument, not an implicit one. That argument has not been made with engulfment data, because synaptic engulfment by microglia has not been measured directly in living human brain.

The evidence layers are therefore these. Measured in mouse: microglial engulfment of presynaptic terminals at the peak of a defined pruning window, its dependence on activity, and its dependence on the CR3 and C3 pathway. Supported in mouse genetic models with input and region specificity: roles for several signalling systems, with negative results for others, so the mechanism is a set of contributing pathways rather than a single switch. Hypothesised and discussed but not established in humans: that the same system eliminates synapses in the human cortex, that its disruption explains neurodevelopmental disorders, and that the amount of pruning in a particular period of human life is a meaningful individual difference. The Soteros and Sia review frames the disease link as an implication of the model, which is exactly the right register: a system that eliminates synapses is a plausible contributor to disorders in which synapse numbers are altered, and plausibility is not evidence. There is also a mundane but important limit on the genetic evidence: most of it comes from mice, where a null mutation often produces a phenotype in one circuit and not in another, so a single knockout result generalises poorly across circuits even within the species.

Finally, note the vocabulary trap. Pruning suggests a gardener with a plan. What the data support is a set of local, activity-sensitive, partly redundant recognition and phagocytosis pathways whose net effect during a narrow developmental window is the removal of some inputs. Where the talk of pruning becomes misleading is when it implies a global programme that explains a late maturational phenomenon such as adolescent behavioural change, because that claim requires measures of synapse elimination and of behaviour in the same human subjects, which the current literature does not have.
lessons.example:
Audit one causal claim from this literature and one popular claim derived from it, using the same five questions.

Claim one, from the primary study: microglia eliminate synapses in the developing retinogeniculate system. The audit proceeds by asking for the type of evidence at each link. Engulfment is shown by tracer labelling plus the lysosomal marker plus immuno-electron microscopy, which is direct evidence that terminals are inside microglia, but it does not show that the internalised material would otherwise have formed functional synapses; the missing control would be a measure of synapse survival in the absence of engulfment. Activity dependence is shown by manipulating activity, so the link between competition and removal is supported. Causality is shown by disrupting the CR3 and C3 pathway and observing sustained deficits in connectivity, which is the strongest step in the chain because it manipulates the presumed mechanism rather than correlating with it. Quantification rests on small per-group samples, three mice per age in the analysis shown, so the appropriate conclusion is that the effect is well-established within this preparation and that replication in other preparations and at other ages would strengthen the general claim.

Claim two, from popular summaries: microglia prune synapses during human adolescence, and altered pruning explains adolescent risk-taking. The audit's arithmetic is the timescale comparison: the demonstrated window is about the first ten postnatal days in the mouse, and human development spans years, so the human timeline is at least two orders of magnitude longer; ten days against a ten-year span gives about 365 as a scaling illustration. Then the evidential question: what measurement in humans corresponds to the mouse engulfment measurement? The answer is none in the current literature, because the human evidence is post-mortem anatomy and gene association rather than measures of elimination rate in living tissue. Finally the behavioural step: even if human pruning rates were measured, linking them to risk-taking requires a within-person design with both measures, adequate reliability for individual differences, and a demonstration that the association is not produced by the same pubertal changes that drive both.

Now a numeric sensitivity check that applies to any single small study in this area. If a per-group sample of three is used to compare two groups, the normal approximation to the power of a two-sided test at an alpha of 0.05 gives about nine per cent power for an effect of half a standard deviation, about 23 per cent for one standard deviation, and about 69 per cent for two standard deviations. That calculation is an approximation rather than an exact result for the t-test with three per group, and it should not be used to dismiss a result that was statistically significant; its purpose is different. It tells you that small studies in this field are informative mainly about large effects, and that the absence of an effect in one small study is uninformative, so the right posture is to look for independent replications and for manipulations of different mechanism rather than to treat any single paper as decisive.

Put the audit together as a review sentence. A defensible summary reads: in mice, microglia engulf retinogeniculate inputs during a defined postnatal window, the process depends on neural activity and on complement receptor signalling, and disrupting that signalling changes connectivity; in humans, the corresponding elimination rate has not been measured, so claims about human adolescent pruning are hypotheses that rest on the mouse mechanism plus anatomical and genetic associations.
lessons.question: A news article states that microglia prune the human adolescent brain, citing the mouse retinogeniculate study. What is the most accurate correction?
lessons.answer: The mouse study demonstrates engulfment of retinal inputs during a postnatal pruning window of a few days with dependence on complement signalling, but synaptic engulfment has not been measured in living human brain, so the human claim is an extrapolation across species, timescale and measurement method.
lessons.distractor: The mouse study is irrelevant to humans because the visual system differs between species and the two eyes compete for territory only in rodents.
lessons.correction: The dismissal goes too far in the opposite direction. The signalling molecules involved, including complement components and phagocytic receptors, have human counterparts, and the general principle that developing circuits eliminate excess connections through activity-dependent competition is supported across mammals, including the neuromuscular junction account in the textbook reading. What the mouse study does not supply is the human measurement: engulfment was shown by tracer labelling, a lysosomal marker and immuno-electron microscopy in mouse tissue at postnatal day 5, and nothing equivalent has been done in living human brain. There is also a timescale problem: pruning in the mouse lateral geniculate nucleus is largely complete by about postnatal day 10, whereas human development unfolds over years, so the two timelines cannot be transferred without an argument. The strongest correction therefore names all three gaps, species, measurement and timescale, and notes what would close them, namely a human measure of synapse elimination with acceptable reliability, paired with the behavioural variable of interest in the same subjects, and a design that can rule out the pubertal processes that would drive both.

depth.definitions: Terms. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, with phagocytic machinery that allows them to engulf cells and cellular material; like peripheral macrophages they express receptors that recognise opsonins. Opsonisation is the coating of a target with molecules that mark it for recognition and engulfment; in this literature the complement protein C3 is the opsonin and complement receptor 3 (CR3) is the microglial receptor. Complement is a cascade of immune proteins; C1q initiates the classical pathway and C3 is a central component, so manipulating C1q or C3 interrupts the same route at different points. Eat-me, find-me and do-not-eat signals are shorthand for the recognition logic of phagocytosis: a target-marking signal, a recruitment signal for the phagocyte, and an inhibitory signal that prevents engulfment. Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a lipid that becomes exposed on the outer membrane leaflet and serves as an eat-me signal. Engulfment is the internalisation of material, measured histologically as colocalisation with a lysosomal marker such as CD68, and it is a different quantity from synapse elimination, which is a loss of functional connections. The retinogeniculate system is the projection from retinal ganglion cells to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, the classic preparation for studying competition between the two eyes. Prerequisites: lessons 42 and 63 on development and critical periods, and lesson 28 on necessity and sufficiency.
depth.mechanism:
In the rodent retinogeniculate system the sequence runs as follows: retinal ganglion cell axons from both eyes initially overlap extensively; spontaneous and then light-driven activity produces competition; the losing inputs are eliminated; and after the first postnatal week each relay cell is dominated by one or a few inputs. Microglia participate in this process by contacting and engulfing presynaptic material, concentrated at the peak of pruning rather than at earlier or later ages, in synapse-rich regions rather than in the non-synaptic optic tract, and dependent on activity, since reducing activity reduces engulfment.

The recognition logic adds a second layer. Complement proteins can opsonise targets, and microglial receptors recognise the opsonins; the reviewed genetic literature reports both positive signals such as C1q and C3 and inhibitory signals such as CD47 and SRPX2, whose removal increases rather than decreases elimination, together with receptors including CR3, GPR56, MERTK and TREM2, each implicated in particular circuits and phases. Two features of that literature constrain what can be concluded. First, results are circuit-specific: GPR56-mediated elimination in hippocampus affected one input pathway and not another onto the same cells, so an effect on synapse density in one region does not license a general statement about the brain. Second, negative results exist and matter: TWEAK deletion did not change retinal terminal phagocytosis in the lateral geniculate nucleus, which shows that not every plausible signal is required.

Limits of the mechanism follow from these facts. Engulfment is measured for a fraction of synapses during a narrow window, so extrapolating an elimination rate from those measurements is not warranted. The pathway redundancy means that single-gene manipulations can produce subtle phenotypes that are easy to miss with small samples, and the same redundancy means a null result in one gene does not falsify the process. Finally, eliminating a synapse and shaping a circuit are different claims: a circuit that loses inputs but produces the same behaviour has not been shown to depend on elimination for its function.
depth.secondExample:
Apply the same audit to the textbook neuromuscular junction account from the UTHealth chapter, which supplies a contrast in mechanism and in evidence style.

There, elimination reduces the number of inputs to a muscle fibre while each remaining input becomes larger and more complex, and the proposed mechanisms are activity-dependent competition, direct competition for target-derived trophic factors, indirect competition in which the target selects among inputs, and possibly a retrograde signal that provokes withdrawal. Cellular and molecular detail is available: elimination involves withdrawal of the presynaptic terminal and loss of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, and receptor clustering changes during development.

Notice what this account has and lacks compared with the microglial account. It has a clearer functional logic, because competition for a limited supply of a target-derived factor is a mechanism with a natural prediction, namely that inputs which receive more activity or more trophic support survive. It is also less dependent on any single knockout, because the competitive framework is defined by the outcome rather than by a molecule. What it lacks, in the sections cited, is a demonstration that any specific immune or phagocytic pathway is required, and this is the honest reason the two stories coexist: elimination at the neuromuscular junction is documented without microglia, and elimination in the retinogeniculate nucleus is documented with them.

The transferable lesson is that more than one elimination mechanism exists, and the correct question about any elimination claim is which circuit and which developmental window it was demonstrated in. A reader who asks that question will treat the phrase synaptic pruning as a category rather than as a mechanism, which is precisely the habit that prevents the human adolescent overclaim. For a third contrast within the same species, note the input-specific hippocampal result: two inputs converging on the same cells differed in whether their elimination depended on one signalling pathway, which means even the same preparation can host more than one elimination logic.
depth.mistake:
The most consequential error here is treating measured engulfment as measured elimination, and then treating elimination as measured behaviour. Engulfment is a histological observation: material from a labelled terminal is found inside a microglial cell, often confirmed by immuno-electron microscopy. Elimination is a loss of functional synapses over time, which requires a different measurement, typically a change in the number of contacts per postsynaptic cell. Behaviour is a third thing again, requiring its own design. Each step can fail independently: internalised material may be debris rather than a functional synapse; a reduction in contacts may be compensated functionally; and a change in contacts may not track the behaviour of interest within individuals. The diagnostic question is what the study measured, and the answer should determine the strength of the verb used in your summary.

A second error is generalising from one circuit because the phrase sounds general. The mouse literature contains input-specific effects within one region and negative results for plausible signals, so a claim of the form microglia prune the developing brain needs a per-circuit demonstration. The diagnostic is to ask which circuit and which developmental window the finding came from, and whether the authors themselves claim generalisation.

A third error, common in popular writing, is to give the mechanism a purpose. A pathway that removes some inputs during a narrow window does not imply that the removal is optimised for anything, and the same molecular machinery participates in injury responses and in clearing debris. Teleological language makes the mechanism feel explanatory while adding no testable content, and it is the reason a phrase like microglia sculpt the brain should be treated as a red flag in a summary rather than as a finding.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You must brief a non-specialist audience on the statement: microglia eliminate synapses in the developing visual system, and this process has been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. Write four bullet points of no more than 30 words each plus one sentence describing the study that would most change your confidence, then compare with the model response.

Model response. Bullet one: in mice, microglia engulf retinal axon terminals during the first postnatal week, concentrated at the peak of the period when the two eyes compete for territory, and this depends on neural activity. Bullet two: the engulfment depends on a specific immune recognition pathway, complement receptor 3 and its ligand C3, and disrupting it changes connectivity, which is why the finding is treated as causal within this preparation. Bullet three: the mechanism is not a single switch; several signalling systems contribute with circuit-specific effects, and at least one plausible candidate tested, TWEAK, made no difference to the early phase. Bullet four: implicating this process in human neurodevelopmental disorders is a hypothesis, because the mouse window is about ten days while human development spans years, and synapse elimination has not been measured in living human brain. Sentence on confidence: confidence would change most with a within-person human study measuring a reliable index of synapse elimination alongside the relevant behavioural or clinical variable, with the design able to rule out pubertal and other common causes. Self-review rubric, four criteria: (1) every claim names the species and the circuit; (2) engulfment, elimination and behaviour are kept distinct; (3) the disorder link is labelled as a hypothesis with the reason stated; (4) the confidence sentence names a specific measurement and design. One point per criterion; a briefing that uses the word pruning without specifying the circuit scores at most two.
depth.summary: Synthesis: synapse elimination during development is documented in more than one way, with competition for trophic support at the neuromuscular junction and with microglial engulfment dependent on complement signalling in the rodent retinogeniculate system; within the microglial account, causality is strongest for the complement receptor pathway in that preparation, generalisation across circuits is constrained by input-specific and negative results, and human application is a hypothesis resting on cross-species analogy rather than measurement. Transfer: for any claim that an immune mechanism shapes the brain, ask for the circuit, the developmental window, the measured quantity, and the control that separates a required mechanism from a correlate, and compute the timescale ratio before transferring a mouse window to a human one.

readings.title: Microglia Sculpt Postnatal Neural Circuits in an Activity and Complement-Dependent Manner (Neuron, 2012), summary and the results on engulfment at the peak of pruning
readings.note: Read the summary for the causal claim (engulfment depends on activity and on CR3 and C3, and disrupting that signalling produced sustained deficits in connectivity) and the first results figure for the quantitative frame: pruning in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus is largely complete by postnatal day 9 or 10, engulfment peaks around day 5, and the quantification shown used three mice per age. Note also the immuno-electron microscopy confirmation localising vesicular glutamate transporter to retinal terminals within microglia.

readings.title: Complement and microglia dependent synapse elimination in brain development (WIREs Mech Dis, 2021), abstract and the sections on complement inhibitors and on disease implications
readings.note: Read for the regulatory logic: complement proteins opsonise targets, microglia phagocytose them, and inhibitors and recruitment signals modulate the process, such that removing inhibitory factors reduces synapse density. Also note the register of the disease section, which presents disorder involvement as an implication of the model rather than as an established mechanism, and use that register in your own summaries.

readings.title: Synaptic Pruning by Microglia: Lessons from Genetic Studies in Mice (Dev Neurosci, 2024), abstract and the sections on eat-me signals and receptor pathways
readings.note: Read for the two constraints that limit generalisation: GPR56-mediated phosphatidylserine-dependent elimination in hippocampus affected one dendritic domain receiving entorhinal input but not another receiving CA3 input, so pruning is input-specific; and TWEAK-deficient mice showed no difference in phagocytosis of retinal terminals in the lateral geniculate nucleus during the early phase, a negative result for a plausible candidate. Also take the inventory of eat-me, find-me and do-not-eat signals for the mechanism paragraph.

readings.title: Synapse Formation, Survival, and Elimination (Neuroscience Online, Section 1 Chapter 9, revised 2024), section 9.17 'Neuronal Survival/Synapse Elimination'
readings.note: Read this textbook section as the non-immune comparison case: elimination at the neuromuscular junction as a reduction in the number of inputs with each remaining input becoming stronger, driven by activity-dependent competition, direct competition for target-derived trophic factors, indirect selection by the target, and possibly a retrograde signal, with withdrawal of the presynaptic terminal and loss of acetylcholine receptors. The absence of any immune cell in this account is the point.
