lessons.title: Computational models as evidence: what fitting, decoding and benchmarking can establish
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to distinguish the claims made by encoding models, decoding models and artificial neural network models of brain data, state the three levels of generalisation that determine how much a modelling result constrains theory, and compute why selecting the best of many models inflates the apparent effect.

Begin with the two model types that are used on measured brain activity. A decoding model is trained to predict the stimulus or the behavioural variable from the activity, and its performance is interpreted as evidence that the information is present in a format the decoder can exploit. An encoding model runs the other way: it predicts the activity from the stimulus, in a specified feature space. Kriegeskorte and Douglas, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), lay out what each can and cannot support, and their list of caveats is the most useful thing in the paper for a reader who wants to use modelling results as evidence rather than as illustration. Three caveats structure this lesson.

The first caveat is the generalisation level. Performance must be evaluated on data that were not used to fit the weights, but new data come in several kinds, and they do not support the same inference. Generalising to new response measurements for the same stimuli tests whether the estimated weights are stable; generalising to new stimuli drawn from the same population tests whether the model captures something general about the stimulus class; generalising to stimuli from a different population tests something stronger again. A result at the first level is compatible with a model that has memorised particular trials, whereas a result at the third level is not. The practical consequence is that the sentence our model decoded the stimulus at 75 per cent accuracy is uninterpretable without the generalisation level, because the same number means different things at each level.

The second caveat is the feature fallacy. An encoding model predicts activity as a linear combination of features chosen by the modeller, such as oriented gratings or semantic dimensions. When such a model fits well, it is tempting to conclude that the brain encodes those features. The fallacy is that many different feature sets span the same linear space, so a good fit cannot in general identify the features; the paper notes that there are infinitely many alternative ways to express the same distribution of activity profiles with different feature sets, and that assuming a prior on the weights reduces the ambiguity without resolving it. What survives the fallacy is the weaker and still useful claim that the representational space contains the information the model indexes.

The third caveat is about comparison. The paper states plainly that significant decoding or encoding performance of a single model does not provide strong constraints for theory and that many models must be tested and inferentially compared for analyses to drive theoretical progress. That sentence has quantitative force, because model comparison introduces a selection problem. If a hundred candidate models are evaluated on the same dataset and the best is reported, the winner is partly a maximum of noise. The expected maximum of a hundred independent standard normal draws is about 2.5 standard deviations, so a selection procedure of that kind can produce an apparent advantage of roughly two and a half standard deviations over the mean with no true difference at all; with a thousand candidates the expected maximum is about 3.24. The remedy is not to stop comparing models but to do it inferentially, with a held-out sample used for comparison and with the comparison itself pre-specified.

Now the numbers that determine how much any accuracy figure constrains anything. Suppose a two-class decoder achieves 70 per cent accuracy, where chance is 50 per cent, and the estimate comes from 100 trials. The standard error of a proportion is the square root of p times one minus p divided by n, which for 0.7 and 100 is 0.0458, so the 95 per cent confidence interval spans about 9 percentage points either side of 70: the point estimate is 0.7 with a half-width of about 0.09. With 20 trials the half-width is about 20 percentage points, and with 1,000 trials it is about 2.8 points. Two consequences follow. Comparisons between conditions with 20 trials per condition cannot resolve differences of a few percentage points, which is within the noise. And a correlation converted to variance has to be squared to be honest about size: a correlation of 0.3 between a model prediction and measured activity accounts for 9 per cent of the variance, 0.5 accounts for 25 per cent, and 0.7 accounts for 49 per cent. Model fits in systems neuroscience are frequently reported in the 0.3 to 0.7 range, and the corresponding variance explained is a useful antidote to the impression of near-perfect prediction that a smooth predicted-versus-measured scatter plot can create.

The third family of models is artificial neural networks, which are used in two quite different ways. Yang and Wang, in a primer in Neuron (2020), present artificial networks as a way to build models of complex behaviours, heterogeneous activity and connectivity, customising architecture and learning to make the model closer to neurobiology, and they supply code so that readers can build such models themselves. Pham, Matsui and Chikazoe, reviewing the correspondence between brains and artificial networks (Biology, 2023), organise the comparison into levels, node, layer, network and behaviour, and note that the field develops quickly with few established standards and practices, which is a warning that benchmarking conventions are not yet settled. When you read that a network predicts brain responses better than another, the questions to ask are which measurement was compared, at which level, whether the comparison was made on data the network never saw, and whether the competing models were matched for size or training data, because a larger model often wins a benchmark for reasons that have nothing to do with brains.

Two boundary cases show what modelling cannot deliver on its own. A model that reproduces a phenomenon without any manipulation is a description, however elegant, and it cannot establish that the mechanism it implements is the one the brain uses, because other mechanisms generate the same phenomenon. And a model fitted to one dataset and reported without cross-validation cannot be evaluated at all, since the fit is guaranteed to be at least as good as the data's own noise structure allows. The result is a division of labour: models generate and constrain hypotheses, and the causal tools of lesson 76 test them.
lessons.example:
Take a concrete modelling claim and audit it, computing the quantities that decide the verdict.

The claim: a deep network trained only on object recognition predicts the responses of neurons in inferotemporal cortex better than a hand-designed model, and the authors conclude that the cortex uses recognition-optimised representations.

Step 1, identify the measurement. The comparison is between predicted and measured response patterns, usually summarised by a correlation or by explained variance. Suppose the reported correlation between the model's layer activations and the measured responses is 0.62 for the network and 0.48 for the hand-designed model, on 60 stimulus presentations. Squaring gives 38 per cent and 23 per cent of variance explained, so the difference the paper is celebrating is 15 percentage points of variance, which is real if the estimate is stable but much smaller than the impression created by the headline that the network predicts the brain.

Step 2, check the noise floor on those estimates. With 60 presentations and a correlation near 0.6, the standard error of a correlation is roughly one minus r squared divided by the square root of n minus three, which for r of 0.6 and n of 60 gives about 0.11. So each estimate carries a margin of roughly a tenth, and the difference of 0.14 between the two models is of the same order as the uncertainty on either. The verdict is not that the finding is false but that the comparison needs more stimuli, more animals or a within-animal inferential treatment, and the paper's own statistics should be checked for that.

Step 3, price the selection. Suppose the paper reports that the network's best layer was chosen by testing all 40 layers and reporting the highest correlation. The expected maximum of 40 noise draws is around 2.3 standard deviations, so part of the reported advantage is the maximum of a selection over layers, and the honest procedure either pre-specifies the layer or corrects for the selection. The same argument applies when a paper benchmarks a dozen architectures and reports the winner.

Step 4, interrogate the mapping. The comparison requires a correspondence between a layer and a brain area, and the review of brain-to-network comparisons organises such correspondences at node, layer, network and behavioural levels with few established standards, so the reader must ask how the brain region was chosen, whether the layer was chosen using the same data, and whether competing models were matched in parameter count and training data. If the network saw a thousand times more images than a human does in the relevant period, the claim that the brain has optimised the same objective needs an argument about the objective rather than about accuracy.

Step 5, state what the result means. A defensible conclusion reads: on this stimulus set and with this measure, representations formed by a recognition-trained network were more similar to recorded responses than representations from a hand-designed model, which constrains the class of computations that could produce the measured responses; whether the cortex implements recognition-like optimisation requires a test in which the two models make different predictions about a new measurement, and that test has not been run.
lessons.question: A paper reports that a decoding model predicts a subject's intended movement direction from neural activity with 75 per cent accuracy in a two-choice task, using 30 trials per condition, and concludes that the population encodes the intention to move. What is the main limitation of the claim?
lessons.answer: The estimate is imprecise at that sample size and the inference is about information present rather than about mechanism, so the result supports decodability of the variable in that population while the confidence interval spans roughly 15 percentage points either side of the estimate.
lessons.distractor: The main limitation is that decoding cannot distinguish between information that is causally used by the brain and information that is merely present, so the result proves nothing about the population at all.
lessons.correction: The over-correction in the second answer throws away a real result. Decoding does establish something: the trained decoder was able to recover the variable from the activity better than chance, which is evidence that information about the variable is present in the population in a format that a linear or non-linear readout can exploit. What it does not establish is that the brain uses that information or that the population generates the behaviour, and the distinction is the one the source draws between information present and mechanism. But the second question to ask is arithmetic rather than conceptual: with 30 trials per condition and an accuracy of 0.75, the standard error is the square root of 0.75 times 0.25 divided by 30, which is about 0.079, so the 95 per cent interval spans roughly 16 percentage points either side, from about 59 to 91 per cent. At that precision, the study can support the qualitative claim that the variable is decodable and cannot support fine comparisons between conditions or claims about how much information is present. The complete assessment therefore combines the conceptual point with the precision calculation, and it recommends what the working example recommends: state the generalisation level, increase the sample, and treat mechanism as a separate question requiring perturbation.

depth.definitions: Terms. An encoding model predicts brain activity from a stimulus representation; a decoding model predicts the stimulus or behaviour from brain activity. The generalisation level is the class of new data on which performance is measured: new measurements for the same stimuli, new stimuli from the same distribution, or stimuli drawn from a different distribution. Cross-validation is the practice of fitting on one part of the data and evaluating on held-out parts; double dipping occurs when the same data are used to select a feature or model and to estimate its performance, which biases the estimate upward. The feature fallacy is the inference from a good fit of a feature-space model to the conclusion that the brain encodes those particular features, an inference blocked by the fact that alternative feature sets span the same space. Representational similarity analysis compares structures of dissimilarities between conditions, using a cross-validated estimator to remove bias from noise. An artificial neural network here means a trained network whose internal representations are compared with brain measurements; when the comparison is claimed to be hierarchical, the correspondence is asserted at node, layer, network or behavioural levels. Effect size in this context is usually a correlation or an explained-variance figure, and its square is the proportion of variance accounted for. Prerequisites: lessons 29 and 30 on reverse inference and evidence arguments.
depth.mechanism:
The reason these models have limited evidential force is structural, and it helps to see it as three separate filters.

The fitting filter. Weights are estimated by minimising error on a training set, and error on that set is an optimistic estimate of performance. Held-out evaluation removes the optimism for the specific partitioning used, and cross-validation averages over partitions, but it does not remove selection effects from choosing the model, the features or the layer that performed best. That is where the expected-maximum arithmetic becomes relevant: if you compare many candidates on the same data, the best performer's advantage includes a component that is the maximum of noise, whose size grows with the number of candidates.

The interpretation filter. A successful fit constrains the class of functions that could map stimuli to responses, and only under additional assumptions does it identify the features. The source states that there are infinitely many alternative ways to express the same distribution of activity profiles with different feature sets, and that a prior on weights narrows but does not close the ambiguity. So the safe reading is about the space of representations, and the unsafe reading is about the specific vocabulary the modeller chose. This matters when a paper reports that its model captures a semantic space, because a different basis with the same span would fit equally well.

The correspondence filter, which applies to networks compared with brains. Choosing which layer corresponds to which area, and which measurement constitutes the comparison, are decisions that can be made after seeing the data. The review of these methods notes the levels at which correspondence is asserted and the absence of settled standards, which is a statement about the maturity of the practice rather than about its value. A benchmark win therefore licenses the claim that this model's representations are closer to these measurements than that model's, under this comparison, which is narrower than the claim that the brain implements this architecture.

The division of labour that results is straightforward: models are hypothesis-generating and hypothesis-constraining devices, and causal manipulations are the test. A model that makes a novel prediction which survives an independent measurement has constrained theory; a model that fits well and makes no risk-bearing prediction has illustrated it.
depth.secondExample:
Apply the same three filters to a radically different kind of model, so that the reasoning transfers beyond neural networks: a simple normative model, such as the claim that a behaviour is well described by a Bayesian observer that combines a noisy sensory likelihood with a prior.

The fitting filter behaves the same way. The model has parameters, usually the noise level and the prior width, and fitting them to behaviour guarantees some goodness of fit; the question is whether the fit was evaluated on held-out data and whether the number of parameters was taken into account in the comparison, since a flexible model will beat a rigid one on training data and may lose on held-out data.

The interpretation filter is where this model class differs, and the difference is instructive. For a Bayesian observer, the mapping from parameters to behaviour is usually many-to-one in a specific way: a change in the prior can be mimicked by a change in the likelihood, so a good fit does not identify which component changed. This is the same ambiguity as the feature fallacy in a different mathematical costume, and the practical remedy is the same: find conditions in which the two interpretations predict different behaviour, and test them.

The correspondence filter has no direct analogue, because a normative model does not claim to be the brain's implementation; it claims that behaviour is consistent with an optimal strategy given assumptions. That claim is weaker and it is honest about being weaker, which is why normative models are good at organising phenomena and poor at settling mechanism.

The contrast with a network benchmark is useful in the other direction too. A network that predicts responses better than a simpler model gains plausibility as a description but faces an identifiability problem when it is large, since many weight configurations produce nearly the same responses. In both cases the question to ask is what distinguishes this model from its competitors, and whether the distinguishing prediction has been tested. When that question has an answer, a modelling paper can carry a strong claim; when it does not, the paper is a demonstration of fitting skill.
depth.mistake:
The most common error in reading modelling papers is the inference from prediction to identification: the model predicts the data, therefore the brain computes what the model computes. The prediction establishes only that the measured responses lie in the class of functions the model can produce, and the source's feature-fallacy argument shows that within even a restricted linear class, alternative vocabularies fit equally well. The diagnostic question is what the model predicts that a rival model does not, and whether that prediction has been tested on new data.

A second error is to read accuracy figures without a noise floor. A decoder at 70 per cent with 20 trials per condition has an interval spanning about 40 percentage points, so the number is compatible with nearly anything above chance; the same number with 1,000 trials spans under 6 points and is worth comparing across conditions. The corrective habit is to compute the standard error before interpreting a difference, and to ask for the generalisation level at which the number was obtained.

A third error is to treat a benchmark ranking as a mechanism. Rankings depend on the comparison set, the size of the models, the amount of training data and the choice of the measurement, so a win is a statement about a specific benchmark. The correction is to ask whether the competing models were matched and whether the comparison was pre-specified or chosen after seeing results.

A fourth error is subtler and concerns null results. A model that fails to fit can fail because it is wrong, because the measurement is unreliable, because the feature space lacks the relevant dimension, or because the fitting procedure converged poorly. Because these alternatives are not distinguished by the fit statistic, a modelling null result is weak evidence about the brain unless the model class is demonstrated to have the capacity to capture the phenomenon.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are given a paper claiming that a network's middle layers best match human brain responses, with a peak correlation of 0.55 in the middle of the network and a lower correlation for both early and late layers, described as a hierarchical correspondence. Write five checks that would decide whether the claim can be read as a hierarchical correspondence, then compare with the model response.

Model response. Check one, generalisation: was the correlation computed on held-out stimuli, and is the generalisation level stated, meaning new measurements for the same stimuli, new stimuli from the same distribution, or stimuli from a new distribution? Check two, selection: were the compared layers and the compared brain regions chosen before or after inspecting the results, and how many comparisons were made? Check three, precision: on how many stimuli and how many participants was each correlation estimated, and what is the standard error, since a correlation of 0.55 estimated on a few dozen presentations cannot support a peak-versus-adjacent comparison that differs by a few hundredths? Check four, model matching: were the competing models matched for parameter count and training experience, and would a smaller model with the same objective achieve a similar match? Check five, prediction: does the claimed correspondence make a novel prediction, for example about a measurement or a manipulation not used in fitting, and has that prediction been tested? Self-review rubric, five criteria, one point each: held-out evaluation with an explicit generalisation level; pre-specified comparisons with the number reported; precision computed and compared with the claimed peak; model matching addressed; a novel prediction identified and tested. Four or five points means the claim is worth taking as a constraint on theories of the region; two or fewer means it is a descriptive similarity finding.
depth.summary: Synthesis: models constrain theories only to the extent that they generalise beyond their fitting data, that their features are not read as identified by a good fit, and that they beat rivals under conditions that were not chosen after seeing the results. Accuracy figures live inside confidence intervals that depend on the number of trials, correlations must be squared to be read as variance explained, and comparisons across many candidates inflate the winner by an expected maximum that grows with the number of candidates. Artificial networks compared with brains extend the same logic with an additional ambiguity, namely the mapping between model levels and brain measurements. Transfer: for any model-based claim, find the risk-bearing prediction, compute the noise floor on the number, and ask what was pre-specified. Then hand the prediction to the causal toolbox of lesson 76, because that is where the claim gets tested.
