visual.title: Three filters a modelling claim must pass, with the arithmetic at each
visual.description: A funnel diagram. Claims enter at the top and pass through three labelled filters in sequence, each with a worked number beside it. Claims that emerge at the bottom are labelled as constraints on theory; claims that do not are labelled as descriptions or demonstrations.
steps: Entry row: three claim types, namely the model predicts the responses, the model decodes the stimulus, and the model beats its rivals, each drawn as a card entering the funnel.

Filter 1 GENERALISATION: three gates labelled new measurements for the same stimuli, new stimuli from the same distribution, and stimuli from a new distribution, with the note that a result at the first gate is compatible with memorisation while a result at the third is not.

Filter 2 INTERPRETATION: a diagram of two different feature sets spanning the same space, labelled FEATURE SET A and FEATURE SET B, both fitting the same activity profiles, with the caption that a good fit does not identify the vocabulary.

Filter 3 COMPARISON: a panel of many candidate models ranked by score, with the winner circled and the expected maximum of 100 noise draws marked at about 2.5 standard deviations and of 1,000 draws at about 3.24.

Precision stamp: an accuracy of 0.70 drawn with three confidence intervals, at 20 trials spanning about 20 points, at 100 trials spanning about 9 points, and at 1,000 trials spanning about 3 points, with the caption that only the last supports fine comparisons.
Effect-size ruler: a scale converting correlations to variance explained, marked at 0.3 for 9 per cent, 0.5 for 25 per cent and 0.7 for 49 per cent.

Output row: two exit boxes, one labelled CONSTRAINS THEORY, for claims that passed all three filters and made a risk-bearing prediction, and one labelled DESCRIBES THE DATA, for the rest, with a note that testing the prediction is the job of the causal tools in lesson 76.

lessons.title: Capstone: designing a study that could actually refute a circuit claim
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to take a one-sentence claim about a circuit, convert it into a design with stated controls, compute the sample the design needs, pre-specify the analysis, and write the interpretation that each possible outcome would license. This capstone draws on every lesson in this level and on the earlier levels it continues.

The claim to work with is deliberately typical: activity in the projection from the prelimbic cortex to the nucleus accumbens is necessary and sufficient for cue-driven reward seeking. It contains four distinct assertions, and the first step of any design is to separate them. Sufficiency: activating the projection increases reward seeking. Necessity: suppressing the projection reduces reward seeking. Specificity: the effect is attributable to this projection rather than to the brain region, the cell type or the general arousal of the animal. And mechanism: the effect operates through the projection's influence on its targets rather than through an unintended consequence of the manipulation. Lessons 28 and 29 supplied the logic; lessons 76 and 77 supplied the instruments and their artifacts; lesson 79 supplied the standard for the modelling component.

Step one is to operationalise the measurement before choosing any manipulation. Reward seeking needs a definition with a number attached: for example, the number of responses in a cue-reward association task, or the latency to enter a reward-paired zone, measured over a stated session length, with a stated reliability. The reliability estimate matters because an unreliable measure caps every effect you can detect: an observed association equals the true association scaled by the square root of the reliability, so with a reliability of 0.5 a true correlation of 0.4 appears as about 0.283, and with a reliability of 0.7 it appears as about 0.335. Reporting the reliability of the primary outcome is not bureaucracy; it is the difference between an effect that failed to replicate and an effect that could never have been detected.

Step two is to select designs for the two directions of the claim, because they are not symmetrical. Sufficiency is tested by activation, most naturally with light, and the controls that lesson 76 requires are a sham-illumination condition in animals without opsin, a temperature estimate at the stated power and duty cycle, and where feasible a second opsin producing the same voltage change through different ions. Necessity is tested by suppression, with light or with a ligand, and the controls required differ: for optogenetic suppression, the same opsin-free and thermal controls; for chemogenetic suppression, a receptor-free group receiving the ligand, a vehicle condition in receptor-expressing animals, and a dose-response establishing that the working dose is behaviourally effective while a lower dose is subthreshold, because the pharmacological literature shows that systemic ligand produces its effects substantially through a conversion product with a broad receptor profile.

Step three is to specify the specificity controls that separate this projection from its alternatives. Three are usually needed. A region-only control compares manipulating the region with manipulating the projection fibres, which addresses the possibility that any local manipulation would do. A cell-type control compares populations within the same region, which addresses the possibility that the effect reflects a general class of projection rather than this one. And a behavioural control shows that the effect is not a general change in movement, motivation or arousal, which is where the striatal rotational artifact documented for illumination is relevant: the artifact produced a directed behavioural bias, so a general-activity explanation must be measured and excluded rather than assumed away.

Step four is the power calculation, done before the experiment rather than after. Using the normal approximation for a two-group comparison with 80 per cent power and a two-sided alpha of 0.05, detecting an effect of 0.2 standard deviations requires about 393 animals per group, 0.3 requires about 175, 0.5 requires about 63, 0.8 requires about 25 and 1.0 requires about 16. The same arithmetic run backwards is more informative for planning: a study with 40 animals per group has about 14 per cent power for a 0.2 standard deviation effect and about 61 per cent for 0.5, which means that a null result from such a study is compatible with an effect that would matter. Say which effect size you are powered to detect, and justify it from the behaviour's variability rather than from convention.

Step five is the pre-specification. Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven and Mellor, in a colloquium paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2018), argue that the distinction between postdiction and prediction is appreciated conceptually but not respected in practice, and that ordinary biases such as hindsight bias make the mistake hard to avoid; preregistration makes the distinction visible. Kiyonaga and Scimeca, in Trends in Neurosciences (2019), describe the Registered Report route, in which the protocol and analysis plan are peer reviewed and accepted in principle before data collection, and list what a thorough report must do: delineate confirmatory hypotheses, demonstrate sufficient statistical power, and ensure reproducibility and replicability. For a project of this kind, the confirmatory set should be small and stated in advance, with the rest labelled exploratory.

Step six is the analysis plan, and it has four components. State the primary outcome and its test, and put everything else in a ranked secondary list. State how multiplicity will be handled, computing the problem first: ten independent tests at an alpha of 0.05 give a family-wise error rate of one minus 0.95 to the tenth power, which is 0.4013, so an uncorrected set of ten tests has a 40 per cent chance of at least one false positive. State the exclusion criteria and the stopping rule in advance. And state how the two key artifacts will be measured rather than assumed: tissue temperature for illumination, and receptor engagement for the chemogenetic arms.

Step seven is the interpretation ladder, written before the data arrive, with one branch per outcome. If activation increases the behaviour and suppression decreases it, with all artifact controls passing, the claim of necessity and sufficiency for this projection, at the timescales tested, is supported in this preparation. If activation changes the behaviour but suppression does not, sufficiency without necessity is supported, which is a common and legitimate result that rules out one of the two original assertions. If suppression produces a deficit but the receptor-free ligand group also shows one, the chemogenetic arm is uninterpretable and the necessity claim must rest on the optogenetic arm alone. If the activation effect disappears with a second, ion-swapped opsin, an ion-specific artifact is indicated. And if the primary outcome shows no effect while a secondary outcome does, the honest report is a null on the primary with an exploratory finding, which is a different kind of claim and must be labelled as such.

Step eight is hedging the descriptive statistics, the part that lesson 77 should have made routine. If single-unit recordings accompany the behaviour, report the probe geometry, the detection threshold, the sorting method, cluster acceptance criteria with at least two metric families, a population-level false discovery rate estimate and a drift check, because predicted false discovery rates in public datasets ranging from about 3 to 50 per cent mean that absolute rate claims need an error bar. If a model is fitted to the result, report held-out performance at a stated generalisation level, avoid reading the fitted feature set as identified, and state what the model predicts that its rivals do not. Ellis, writing in eNeuro (2022), argues that replicability problems in preclinical neuroscience arise from questionable research practices, misinterpretation of p-values and low power, and that changing incentives, with registered reports as the most immediately practical step, is necessary; the same paper emphasises comprehensive reporting of the conditions that could make a result sensitive, which for animal work includes the strain, the housing, the season and the experimenter. Those variables look mundane until you try to replicate.

A note on scope, which matters more in this subject than in most. Everything in this capstone concerns how to design and read research. Nothing here is advice about any person or any treatment, and the interpretation of an individual's results belongs with a qualified professional.
lessons.example:
Work the design through with the arithmetic at each step, exactly as you would write it in a Registered Report.

Claim restatement. Confirmatory hypothesis one: activating prelimbic-to-accumbens projection terminals increases cue-driven reward seeking relative to sham illumination. Confirmatory hypothesis two: suppressing the same terminals decreases it. Everything else is exploratory.

Measurement. Primary outcome: responses per 20-minute session in a cue-reward task, averaged over the final three of five training sessions. Reliability: the intraclass correlation across sessions for this measure in pilot data is assumed to be 0.7, which attenuates a true correlation of 0.4 to about 0.335, using the square root of 0.7, which is about 0.837. Reported as an assumption with pilot estimates to be supplied.

Power. The minimum effect of interest is 0.5 standard deviations in responses per session, chosen because smaller effects would not change the conclusions the field draws. With 80 per cent power and a two-sided alpha of 0.05, a two-group comparison requires about 63 animals per group; the study will therefore use 64 per group, giving about 80 per cent power. If only 40 animals per group were available, power for that effect falls to about 61 per cent, and power for a 0.2 standard deviation effect to about 14 per cent, which would make a null uninformative, so the report states that 40 per group is acceptable only with a pre-registered equivalence test and an explicit acknowledgement of the larger effect the design can detect.

Sufficiency arm and its controls. Light at a stated power and duty cycle, with four conditions in the same animals: opsin with light, opsin without light, no opsin with light, and a second opsin producing the same voltage effect through different ions with light. Tissue temperature measured or modelled at the fibre tip, and the expected rate effect computed from the temperature coefficient: at 10 milliwatts the inferred rise is about two thirds of one degree Celsius, taking the power-to-temperature relationship from lesson 76 as the basis, which with a temperature coefficient of 2 corresponds to a rate change of about 5 per cent, so any observed behavioural effect must exceed that margin to be attributed to the opsin.

Necessity arm and its controls. Optogenetic suppression with the same opsin-free and temperature conditions. Chemogenetic suppression with four groups: receptor plus ligand at the working dose, receptor plus vehicle, no receptor plus ligand, and receptor plus a quarter of the working dose, with the last group providing the dose-response evidence that the working dose is effective while a lower one is subthreshold. Because systemic ligand acts partly through a conversion product, the receptor-free ligand group is the control that decides whether the arm is interpretable.

Specificity controls. A region-only manipulation in a separate cohort; a comparison projection from the same region to a different target; and a movement and arousal panel, namely locomotion, reaction time to a neutral cue and consumption of freely available reward, so that a general explanation can be tested rather than assumed away.

Analysis. Primary test: a mixed-effects model on responses per session with condition as a fixed effect and animal as a random effect, with the confirmatory alpha of 0.025 for each of the two hypotheses. Multiplicity: the two confirmatory tests are the extent of the correction, with a note that the family-wise error rate for ten uncorrected tests would be 0.40, so secondary outcomes are reported with a stated correction and labelled exploratory. Exclusions: animals not expressing the construct above a stated threshold, sessions with equipment faults, and a maximum of one excluded session per animal, with the rule written before data collection. Robustness: the primary analysis repeated after winsorising the responses, and repeated excluding the highest-response animal, both pre-specified.

Interpretation ladder. All controls passing with both directions significant: the projection is necessary and sufficient for the behaviour at the timescales tested, in this preparation. Sufficiency only: report sufficiency and state that the necessity claim was not supported. Receptor-free ligand group showing a behavioural effect: report the chemogenetic arm as uninterpretable and rely on the optogenetic direction. Second-opsin condition differing: report an ion-specific artifact and abandon the effect claim pending a different control. Primary null with a secondary effect: report a null on the primary and label the secondary as exploratory, with the effect size and its interval given so that a future meta-analysis can use it.
lessons.question: Your preregistered protocol specifies a 20-minute session and a fixed light power, but after the first cohort you discover that the hormone cycle stage changes the behavioural baseline substantially. What is the best course?
lessons.answer: Report the deviation transparently, keep the preregistered primary analysis as specified, add the cycle stage as a pre-specified covariate in an explicitly labelled exploratory analysis and in a clearly reported amended protocol for the remaining animals, rather than changing the plan silently or discarding the first cohort.
lessons.distractor: Silently add the covariate to the main model, because the analysis is still statistically valid and reporting the change would only invite the impression that the study was poorly planned.
lessons.correction: The second option is the exact practice that preregistration exists to prevent. It is not that adding a covariate is wrong; it is that changing the analysis after seeing results converts a prediction into a postdiction, and the credibility of the finding depends on the reader being able to tell which of the two they are being shown. The literature on preregistration treats the discovery of assumption violations mid-study as one of the standard challenges and expects it to be documented rather than absorbed into the analysis: the protocol's value depends on the record of what was specified before data collection and what changed afterwards. The correct handling has three parts. First, keep the preregistered primary analysis as the confirmatory test, because the protocol was reviewed and fixed on the basis of the design at that time. Second, add the covariate in a clearly labelled exploratory analysis so the reader sees both results and can judge whether the conclusion depends on the adjustment. Third, amend the protocol for the remaining animals with a dated record of the change and its justification, which turns the amendment into a second pre-specification rather than a repair. There is also a scientific reason to prefer this route: if cycle stage produces a large baseline shift, the study's power may be lower than planned, and the reviewer needs to know that the estimate of the effect size may change. A final option worth naming is to pause, hold the first cohort, and analyse it together with the amended protocol only after consulting the review venue, which is the process the Registered Report format supports.

depth.definitions: Design vocabulary used in this capstone. A confirmatory hypothesis is stated before data collection and tested by a pre-specified analysis; an exploratory analysis generates hypotheses and cannot confirm them. Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it exists, and it depends on the effect size, the alpha level, the variance and the design. The minimum effect of interest is the smallest effect that would change the conclusion, and it is what a power calculation should be run on. A within-subject design compares conditions inside the same animal, which removes between-animal variance from the comparison and therefore needs fewer animals, at the cost of order and carry-over effects that must be controlled. Attenuation is the reduction of an observed association by the unreliability of the measures, and the correction uses the square root of the reliability. Multiplicity is the inflation of false positive risk when several tests are run, with the family-wise error rate for ten independent tests at an alpha of 0.05 being about 0.40. A stopping rule states in advance when data collection ends, which prevents collecting until significance appears. Preregistration is a dated, frozen record of the plan, and a Registered Report is the version in which the plan is peer reviewed and accepted before data collection. Prerequisites: lessons 61 to 70 on testing claims, and lesson 28 on necessity and sufficiency.
depth.mechanism:
Why each element of the design is necessary rather than decorative is best seen as an inference chain with one link per control. From the observation that illumination changes the behaviour, the first link is whether the opsin caused the change: an opsin-free animal that received the same illumination tests that link, and a temperature measurement tests the alternative pathway in which heat changes excitability, with the size of that alternative computed rather than guessed. From the observation that illumination of opsin-expressing tissue changed the behaviour, the second link is whether the change came from the targeted population rather than from anything else illuminated: cell-type and region controls test that link, and the second-opsin control tests the pathway in which the specific ion conductance, rather than the voltage change, produced the effect. From the observation that suppression produced a deficit, the third link is whether the suppression was achieved by the intended receptor rather than by the ligand acting elsewhere: the receptor-free ligand group and the dose-response test that link, and the conversion pharmacology is what makes them mandatory rather than optional. The fourth link runs from the circuit to the behaviour: whether the effect is a general change in motor output, motivation or arousal is tested by the movement and arousal panel.

Each link has a characteristic failure mode, and the design's strength is the product of its links, not the sum. A study with excellent controls on the first three links and none on the fourth can still be wrong about the circuit-to-behaviour step, and a study with a weak first link can be wrong about everything downstream. This is why a pre-registered interpretation ladder is worth writing: it forces the analyst to say in advance which outcome licenses which link, and it makes the difference between sufficiency and necessity a stated component rather than a rhetorical flourish. The limits are equally structured: even a fully controlled study supports its claim only for the species, preparation, timescale and dose used, which is why the reporting recommendations for animal research emphasise documenting the conditions that could make the result sensitive.
depth.secondExample:
Contrast the animal circuit design with a human study of an analogous claim, where the tools differ and so do the available inferences.

Suppose the claim is that activity in a particular frontal network is necessary for a cognitive control behaviour in people. Optogenetics is unavailable, so necessity must be tested by other means: transcranial magnetic stimulation can disrupt a cortical region transiently, which is an acute perturbation whose behavioural consequences bear on necessity, but its spatial resolution is coarse and its effect depends on the state of the cortex at the moment of stimulation. Functional imaging can show that a region's activity covaries with performance, which is a correlation whose direction is ambiguous, and lesions provide strong necessity evidence with poor localisation and long-lasting compensation.

Design the human study with the same eight steps and note where they bind differently. Measurement: the behavioural index needs reliability across sessions, which for many cognitive tasks is lower than experimenters expect, and attenuation applies as it did in the animal case. Power: the same arithmetic holds, and the effect sizes in this literature are often in the 0.2 to 0.5 range, which implies hundreds of participants for well-powered between-group designs; within-participant designs are therefore the norm. Controls: the analog of the opsin-free condition is stimulation at a control site, and the analog of the heating artifact is the non-specific effect of stimulation on attention and somatosensation, which must be measured rather than asserted. Specificity: the analog of the cell-type control is the comparison of two sites with different connectivity, and the analog of the movement panel is the exclusion of a speed-accuracy trade-off, which is the persistent confound in reaction-time studies. Pre-specification: identical logic, and the same reasoning about multiplicity, with a family-wise error rate of about 0.40 for ten uncorrected tests.

The transferable point is that the checklist is invariant while the instruments change, and that the replacement of a tool always requires naming the artifact the new tool introduces. In the animal case the artifact is heat or ligand pharmacology; in the human case it is non-specific stimulation effects and the state dependence of the manipulation. A reader who carries the checklist across the two literatures will notice which human claims rest on correlation dressed as necessity, and which animal claims rest on a manipulation whose artifact was never measured.
depth.mistake:
The most frequent error in this area is the silent substitution of hypotheses: a study is designed to test one thing, the data show something else, and the introduction is rewritten so that the paper appears to have tested what it found. The mechanism of the error is hindsight bias, which the preregistration literature identifies explicitly, and the diagnostic is the dated record: what was written before the data were collected, and what was added afterwards. The correction is not to refuse to report the unexpected finding but to label it as exploratory and to keep the confirmatory test as originally specified, so that both are visible.

A second error is running the power calculation on the effect size the study happened to observe, which turns power analysis into a description rather than a plan, and inflates the apparent justification for a small sample. The correction is to state the minimum effect of interest from the behaviour's variability and the field's needs, and to report what the design can detect, including what it cannot.

A third error is treating a control as a formality. A sham condition, a second opsin, a receptor-free ligand group and a movement panel each test one specific link, and running them without measuring the artifact they are meant to bound leaves the link untested. The correction is to name, for each control, the artifact and the size the artifact would have to reach to explain the effect, and to record that number in the protocol.

A fourth error is over-reading a null. A null result from a design powered for a large effect is compatible with a small but real effect, and reporting it as evidence of absence requires either the power calculation that shows the design could have detected the smallest effect of interest, or an equivalence test. Without one of those, a null is a statement about the study rather than about the brain, and the arithmetic for a 40-per-group design detecting 0.2 standard deviations, about 14 per cent power, shows how easily that mistake is made.
depth.application:
Capstone task, done in writing and submitted for review by another student. Produce a one-page protocol for the claim that a named projection is both necessary and sufficient for a named behaviour, containing: the claim split into confirmatory hypotheses; the primary outcome with its reliability estimate; the design for both directions of the manipulation; the control suite with the artifact each control bounds and the size that artifact would need to reach to explain the effect; the power calculation with its stated minimum effect of interest; the multiplicity plan with the computed family-wise error rate for the number of tests proposed; the pre-specified exclusion and stopping rules; and the interpretation ladder with one branch per plausible outcome. Then review another student's protocol using the rubric below and return concrete demands rather than general praise.

Model response outline. Claim split into four assertions with two labelled confirmatory. Primary outcome defined with sessions, averaging rule and reliability. Sufficiency arm with four illumination conditions and a temperature estimate; necessity arm with optogenetic suppression and a chemogenetic arm with receptor-free, vehicle and quarter-dose conditions. Specificity controls for region, projection target and general activity. Power stated as about 63 animals per group for the minimum effect of interest of 0.5 standard deviations, with the numbers for 0.2 and 0.3 given so the reader sees the cost of ambition. Multiplicity plan reporting that ten uncorrected tests would give a family-wise error rate of about 0.40 and stating the correction. Exclusion and stopping rules written as rules with numbers. Interpretation ladder with branches for both-significant, sufficiency-only, chemogenetic-uninterpretable, ion-specific-artifact and primary-null outcomes. Self-review rubric, eight criteria, one point each: (1) claim decomposed into testable assertions; (2) primary outcome with reliability; (3) both directions of manipulation designed; (4) each control paired with an artifact and a magnitude; (5) power calculated for a stated minimum effect of interest; (6) multiplicity computed rather than asserted; (7) exclusion and stopping rules pre-specified; (8) interpretation ladder with at least four branches. A protocol scoring below six is not ready for data collection, and the reviewer's job is to name the two missing criteria and the sentence that would supply each.
depth.summary: Synthesis: a circuit claim becomes science when it is decomposed into testable assertions, bound to a measurement with stated reliability, tested in both directions with controls that bound the specific artifacts of the chosen tools, powered for a stated minimum effect of interest, pre-registered with a multiplicity plan and written interpretation branches, and reported with the descriptive statistics needed for replication. Each element answers one link in the inference chain from manipulation to behaviour, and a claim is only as strong as its weakest link. Transfer: this protocol generalises to any causal claim about a system, including claims in the literature you will read next, and it is the standard you should apply to your own work before you run it, because the cost of the design work is small compared with the cost of an experiment that cannot answer its own question.

readings.title: The preregistration revolution (Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 2018), abstract and the sections on prediction versus postdiction and on practical challenges
readings.note: Read the abstract for the argument that the distinction between postdiction and prediction is appreciated but not respected in practice, and that hindsight bias makes the error hard to avoid, and read the challenge sections for the standard difficulties: changes to procedure during administration, discovery of assumption violations during analysis, preexisting data, and longitudinal studies. The scenario in this lesson's quiz item is one of those challenges.

readings.title: Practical considerations for navigating Registered Reports (Trends Neurosci, 2019), abstract and the figure of practical steps
readings.note: Read for what a thorough Registered Report must do, namely delineate confirmatory hypotheses, demonstrate sufficient statistical power, and ensure reproducibility and replicability. Use the steps as the skeleton of the capstone protocol and the review rubric, and note that the format provides review before data collection, which is what makes the amendment procedure in the quiz item tractable.

readings.title: Questionable Research Practices, Low Statistical Power, and Other Obstacles to Replicability (eNeuro, 2022), abstract, the section on registered reports and the section on reporting for animal research
readings.note: Read the abstract for the account of questionable research practices, misinterpretation of p-values and low power, and for the argument that registered reports are the most immediately practical remedy. Then read the sections on issues specific to animal research to see which conditions need to be reported, since those are the variables the capstone protocol requires you to document.

readings.title: Analytical Transparency and Reproducibility in Human Neuroimaging Studies (J Neurosci editorial, 2018)
readings.note: A short editorial, so read it as a brief statement of a journal's position on analytical transparency, selective reporting and circular inference. Use it to show that the concerns in this lesson are institutional rather than idiosyncratic, and note the editorial's own framing of the series as recommendations for statistical practice.

visual.title: The eight-step protocol as a chain of inference, with the arithmetic attached to each link
visual.description: A vertical chain of eight boxes, each labelled with the design step, the link in the inference chain it secures, and the specific quantity that must be reported. A side column lists the artifact each control bounds, and a bottom ladder shows outcomes mapped to licensed conclusions.
steps: Step 1 DECOMPOSE: one claim card splitting into sufficiency, necessity, specificity and mechanism, with the note that two of the four become labelled confirmatory hypotheses and the rest become exploratory.
Step 2 MEASURE: primary outcome with session length, averaging rule and reliability, drawn with an attenuation arrow showing reliability 0.7 multiplying a true correlation of 0.4 down to about 0.335.
Step 3 MANIPULATE: two arms, activation drawn with four illumination conditions and suppression drawn with optogenetic and chemogenetic variants, each with its control boxes attached.

Step 4 CONTROL: a table of controls with the artifact each bounds and its size, including opsin-free sham, temperature at about 0.067 degrees Celsius per milliwatt with a rate effect of roughly 5 per cent at 10 milliwatts, second opsin with different ions, receptor-free ligand, vehicle, quarter dose, region-only, other projection, and the movement and arousal panel.

Step 5 POWER: a bar chart of animals per group for 80 per cent power at effect sizes 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0 with the values about 393, 175, 63, 25 and 16, and a second bar showing that 40 per group yields about 14 per cent power for 0.2 standard deviations.

Step 6 PRE-SPECIFY: a frozen protocol document with its date, containing confirmatory hypotheses, analysis plan, exclusion rules and stopping rule, with a note that ten uncorrected tests give a family-wise error rate of about 0.40 so the multiplicity plan must be stated.

Step 7 INTERPRET: a ladder of five outcomes, both directions significant, sufficiency only, chemogenetic arm uninterpretable, ion-specific artifact, and primary null with a secondary effect, each mapped to the conclusion it licenses.

Step 8 REPORT: a reporting card listing probe geometry and sorting metrics for any recordings, held-out performance at a stated generalisation level for any model, and the conditions that could make the result sensitive, with the note that the honest report includes what the design could not detect.

questions.prompt: A protocol specifies 30 milliwatts of continuous illumination in striatum for 20 seconds and reports a 20 per cent increase in a motivated behaviour. The methods state that no temperature measurement was made. How should a reviewer respond?
questions.answer: Require either a temperature estimate or an opsin-free and ion-swapped control, because at that power the reported relationship implies a rise of about 2 degrees Celsius with a rate effect of roughly 15 per cent for a temperature coefficient of 2, which is comparable to the reported behavioural effect.
questions.distractor: Reject the study outright, because any tissue heating invalidates optogenetic results and the artifact cannot be bounded after data collection.
questions.correction: The second response is too strong in both directions at once. Heating is a real and documented artifact, but its size depends on power, duty cycle and preparation, and the literature provides a quantitative relationship that allows the concern to be bounded: reported temperature increases scale with power, about 0.2 to 2 degrees over 3 to 30 milliwatts, so 30 milliwatts sits at the top of that range, and the rate consequence of a 2 degree rise with a temperature coefficient of 2 is roughly 15 per cent. That number is the reason the reviewer's demand is reasonable rather than merely cautious: a 20 per cent behavioural effect with a 15 per cent possible thermal contribution is not separable without a control. The bounded concern can be addressed after the fact by adding a temperature measurement in a follow-up cohort, by running the sham condition in opsin-free animals, and by repeating the manipulation with a second opsin that produces the same voltage change through different ions. Discarding the study, by contrast, would discard what may be a real effect.

questions.prompt: You are asked which single additional condition would most strengthen a chemogenetic necessity claim in which receptor-expressing animals received 10 milligrams per kilogram of the ligand and showed a deficit while vehicle controls did not. Which condition, and why?
questions.answer: A receptor-free group receiving the same ligand dose, because the systemically administered ligand produces behavioural effects partly through a conversion product with a broad receptor profile, so the comparison that isolates receptor engagement is the one between animals with and without the receptor at that dose.
questions.distractor: A lower dose of the ligand in the receptor-expressing animals only, because the point of a chemogenetic experiment is to show that the effect scales with the dose in the animals that carry the receptor.
questions.correction: A dose-response is useful, but it does not do the work that the receptor-free group does. If the ligand has off-target actions, then a dose-response in receptor-expressing animals may simply be tracing the off-target pharmacology, since both the intended and unintended effects grow with dose. What isolates the receptor is a comparison in which the receptor is the only difference, which is why the receptor-free animals at the same dose are the decisive control, and why the documented pharmacology of the commonly used ligand matters: it is largely converted in vivo to a compound that crosses the blood-brain barrier and binds endogenous receptors with high affinity, such that a hundred-fold higher ligand dose was equivalent to a subthreshold dose of the conversion product, and higher doses of that product affected control animals too. Within that design, the useful supplementary conditions are the receptor-free group at the working dose and a dose-response demonstrating that a lower dose is behaviourally ineffective, which together show that the working dose acts through the receptor rather than through the ligand's own profile.

questions.prompt: A spike-sorting paper reports that all analysed units had zero interspike-interval violation counts and that the population contains 60 per cent more fast-firing cells than previous papers. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
questions.answer: The violation criterion differentially excludes fast-firing units, because chance short intervals accumulate steeply with firing rate, so a zero-violation filter selects against the very population that seems over-represented and the reported composition may reflect the filter rather than the brain.
questions.distractor: The population contains more fast-firing cells because the new recording method has better electrode impedance and therefore detects more small cells than previous methods.
questions.correction: Impedance and detection improvements are real and worth considering, but they cannot explain the pattern that the answer identifies, which is an arithmetic property of the metric. For a Poisson process with a fixed short-interval window of 1.5 milliseconds observed for 600 seconds, the expected number of such intervals is about 0.9 at a firing rate of 1 per second, about 90 at 10 per second and over 2,000 at 50 per second. A criterion requiring zero violations therefore has a strongly rate-dependent false exclusion, and applying it before comparing compositions biases the comparison. The wider literature reinforces the point: the relationship between violation rate and false discovery rate is highly nonlinear and depends on firing frequency, correlated activity and contaminant count, with predicted median false discovery rates in public datasets spanning roughly 3 to 50 per cent, and single-cluster prediction is unreliable in that analysis. The check to run first is therefore whether the filter was applied uniformly and what proportion of fast-firing units was discarded.

questions.prompt: A sales deck states that a polygenic score predicts a cognitive outcome with a correlation of 0.3 and should be used to tailor interventions to individuals. Which response is most accurate?
questions.answer: A correlation of 0.3 explains about 9 per cent of the variance, so the score shifts group means but cannot resolve individuals, and the published educational evidence found such prediction inferior to parental socioeconomic factors and uninformative once prior achievement was included.
questions.distractor: A correlation of 0.3 is a strong effect for a behavioural outcome, so the score is suitable for tailoring interventions provided it is applied with adequate training data.
questions.correction: The framing of 0.3 as strong is where the reasoning goes wrong. Squaring the correlation gives the proportion of variance shared, so 0.3 corresponds to 9 per cent and leaves 91 per cent to other influences, which is why the distributions of high and low scorers overlap almost completely and why individual prediction fails despite a statistically robust group-level association. The empirical comparison makes the point concrete: in a cohort with schooling records, the polygenic score predicted achievement more poorly than parental socioeconomic factors and added nothing useful once prior achievement was known, and the authors conclude that such scores inform group differences rather than individual prediction. Two further checks belong in the response: prediction accuracy degrades when the target population differs in ancestry from the discovery sample, and a tailored intervention claim requires trial evidence that the intervention works differently at different score values, which is a separate study and a separate requirement.

questions.prompt: A modelling paper reports that its network predicts neural responses with a correlation of 0.55, chosen as the best of 40 layers, on 50 stimulus presentations, and concludes that the region implements the network's computations. Which revision is best?
questions.answer: Report that the network's representations matched the responses at held-out generalisation level, with the selection over layers acknowledged and the precision stated, since a correlation of about 0.55 on that number of presentations carries a margin of roughly a tenth and part of the peak reflects selection among 40 layers.
questions.distractor: Report that the network explains most of the response variance, since a correlation of 0.55 is a strong fit and the layer selection was principled because layers correspond to stages of processing.
questions.correction: The second revision makes two errors in one sentence. Correlations are not variance: 0.55 squared is about 0.30, so roughly 30 per cent of the response variance is accounted for, not most of it. And a peak chosen as the best of 40 candidates is a maximum of a noisy quantity, whose expected value exceeds the mean even with no true difference, around 2.3 standard deviations for 40 candidates in the standard illustration; the honest report either pre-specifies the comparison layer or accounts for the selection. Precision matters for the same reason: with about 50 presentations, the standard error of a correlation near 0.55 is in the region of a tenth, so the ranking of adjacent layers cannot be interpreted. None of this makes the result worthless; the defensible claim is that representations formed by this model were more similar to the measured responses than those of competing models under a stated comparison, which constrains the class of computations without identifying the brain's algorithm.

questions.prompt: A paper claims that a class of neurons performs linear integration, based on a regression of somatic voltage on the number of stimulated spines with a slope of 0.9 millivolts per spine and an intercept of 2 millivolts, fitted across 12 stimulation intensities. You have one extra recording session. Which single manipulation would most directly test the linearity claim, and what would the result look like under a nonlinear mechanism?
questions.answer: Hold the number of stimulated spines constant and move them between one branch and several branches: a linear integrator should produce the same somatic voltage for the same count regardless of arrangement, whereas a supralinear dendritic mechanism should produce a larger response when the inputs share a branch, and blockade of the voltage-dependent conductance should reduce the arranged condition toward the split condition.
questions.distractor: Fit the same regression separately for the proximal and distal halves of the dendritic tree and compare the slopes, because differences in slope between locations are the definition of nonlinear integration.
questions.correction: The second manipulation changes two variables at once, because proximal and distal sites differ in their passive attenuation as well as in their propensity for regenerative events, so a slope difference between halves is consistent with purely passive cable properties and does not isolate nonlinearity. The arrangement manipulation is the sharper test because it holds the input count, the stimulus intensity and the recording site fixed and varies only geometry, and the passive model makes a definite prediction of invariance. The result under a nonlinear mechanism has two parts, and the second part is what makes the test convincing: an arrangement-dependent difference, and the disappearance of that difference when the regenerative conductance is blocked while the linear component remains. A regression slope alone cannot distinguish a nonlinear mechanism from a linear one with site-dependent scaling, which is why the lesson's audit demands a manipulation that the two accounts predict differently.

questions.prompt: Two reviews of the same astrocyte case make opposite recommendations: one concludes that astrocytes are integral synaptic elements, the other that the key release evidence is unreliable. A researcher must decide whether to spend a year on a follow-up experiment. Using the two positions, what design would produce a result that both reviews would have to accept?
questions.answer: A within-preparation design in which the release machinery is disrupted only in astrocytes using a targeting construct whose leak into neurons is quantified, with the receptor on the neuronal side manipulated independently and the synaptic outcome measured in the same animals, so that the result does not depend on the specificity of a single genetic line.
questions.distractor: A larger experiment using the same dnSNARE construct in more animals, because the criticism concerned statistical power rather than the validity of the construct.
questions.correction: The criticism was not about power, and repeating the same design at greater scale would reproduce the same interpretive ambiguity: if the construct also suppresses exocytosis in neurons, then any phenotype remains compatible with a neuronal mechanism, and a larger sample would merely estimate that ambiguous quantity more precisely. The reviews agree that the calcium signal, the anatomical contact and the modulation of some synapses are documented, and they disagree about the vesicular-release step, so the experiment must attack that step's identification rather than its precision. That requires quantifying the targeting construct's leak with a neuronal marker, manipulating the receiving neuron's receptors independently so that the effect can be located on the neuronal side, and measuring the outcome in the same preparation that the manipulation was verified in. A design meeting those three requirements produces evidence whose interpretation does not turn on which review one prefers.

questions.prompt: You are editing a textbook chapter that currently states that critical periods end when perineuronal nets form, and that adult brains therefore cannot change with experience. Two sentences need rewriting. Which pair of sentences is defensible?
questions.answer: Matrix maturation around fast-spiking interneurons is one contributor to the decline of plasticity, alongside changes in inhibition and other factors; and adult experience-dependent change is graded rather than absent, as shown by small reversible ocular dominance shifts after a few hours of monocular deprivation in adults, with larger effects requiring much larger doses.
questions.distractor: Matrix maturation closes critical periods, which is why digesting chondroitin sulfate chains reactivates plasticity; and adult brains retain a latent capacity for change that is released whenever the matrix is removed.
questions.correction: The second pair contains two errors that this level's evidence forbids. First, attributing closure to the matrix as a single cause overstates the case, because the digestion literature supports a constraint role while the genetic literature shows that three of the four tested lecticans are dispensable for the structural marker, and because digestion removes all chondroitin sulfate chains irrespective of sulfation, so the molecular target is unidentified. Second, the claim that adults can change whenever the matrix is removed is a sufficiency claim that the evidence does not support, since the observed adult effects after brief deprivation are small and reversible rather than transformative. The approved pair keeps the mechanism as a contributor, states the graded nature of adult change, and attaches a dose, which is what allows the statement to be compared with experiments rather than merely believed.

questions.prompt: A funding panel receives two proposals about adult human hippocampal neurogenesis. Proposal one will count doublecortin-positive cells in autopsy tissue from 40 donors aged 20 to 80 using one antibody and existing protocols. Proposal two will process surgical and autopsy tissue from the same donors through two protocols, use two immaturity markers plus morphology, and pre-register the counting rules. Which should the panel prefer, and on what reasoning?
questions.answer: Proposal two, because the dispute in this literature turns on identification, processing and quantification rather than on sample size, so a one-marker count under a single protocol would produce another number that cannot be compared with the existing discordant results.
questions.distractor: Proposal one, because a larger donor sample across a wide age range gives a better estimate of the population quantity and will settle the disagreement by accumulating evidence.
questions.correction: Accumulating more of the same measurement does not resolve a disagreement about what the measurement means. The published estimates differ by two to three orders of magnitude, from roughly 700 new cells per day in one method to densities of a few cells per square millimetre and no detected cells in another, which is far beyond what sampling error can explain, so the disagreement lies in identification criteria, tissue processing and quantification. Proposal two attacks those directly by making protocol a within-donor factor, so any difference attributable to processing appears as an internal comparison rather than as a between-study mystery, and by fixing identification rules in advance so that the count is reproducible across laboratories. The age range and sample size of proposal one are reasonable features; the problem is that its output would have the same ambiguity as the studies it is meant to adjudicate.

questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical company proposes to develop a compound that enhances microglial synaptic pruning during adolescence, on the grounds that microglia prune synapses in development and that altered pruning is implicated in psychiatric disorders. As a scientific adviser, what is your primary objection and what evidence would be required to overcome it?
questions.answer: The proposal inverts an unfinished inference chain: engulfment and elimination have been demonstrated in the mouse retinogeniculate system with circuit-specific and sometimes negative results, no measure of synapse elimination exists in living human brain, and disease involvement is presented as an implication of the model rather than an established mechanism, so human efficacy and even the direction of benefit are unsupported.
questions.distractor: The proposal is premature only because the relevant pruning window in humans has not been dated precisely, so the compound should be tested once the adolescent window is defined by imaging studies.
questions.correction: Dating the window would not fix the deeper problem, and the objection must be stated at the level of the claim rather than at the level of scheduling. The evidence supports a mechanism in specific mouse circuits during a window of days, with dependence on activity and on a complement pathway, and with input-specific effects and documented negative results for other candidate signals. Between that and a human therapeutic claim stand several unbridged steps: no human measurement of synaptic engulfment or elimination, no evidence that pruning magnitude is an individual difference that predicts anything, no evidence that increasing pruning would be beneficial rather than harmful, since the disorder literature itself implicates altered pruning in both directions, and no clinical development pathway in which a chronic manipulation of immune function in adolescents could be justified by expectancy alone. The minimum evidence to overcome the objection would be a validated human measure of synapse elimination with acceptable reliability, an association between that measure and the clinical outcome within individuals, and a demonstration that the manipulation moves the measure in the direction associated with better outcomes.

questions.prompt: A preprint reports that a model's middle layer best matches a cortical area, with a correlation of 0.5 that was estimated after averaging 200 trials per participant across 15 participants, and it argues that the correspondence explains the area's function. Meanwhile a recording paper reports that only 40 per cent of its sorted units met an isolation threshold. How do the two reporting problems belong to the same family?
questions.answer: Both are quantification problems in which a summary number is presented without the quantity that bounds it: the model result needs held-out generalisation, an account of how the layer was selected and the precision of a correlation estimated across participants, while the recording result needs the discarded fraction and a population-level error estimate, because both a correlation of 0.5 and a unit count are inferences whose uncertainty is not in the reported figure.
questions.distractor: They belong to the same family because both reflect insufficient sample size, and both would be resolved by collecting more data: more participants in the modelling study and more recording sessions in the electrophysiology study.
questions.correction: More data would help both studies and would still leave both claims uninterpretable if the reporting were unchanged. In the modelling case the issues are selection and generalisation rather than volume: a correlation computed after choosing the best layer is partly a maximum of noise, with an expected maximum of roughly 2.3 standard deviations for 40 candidates, and a peak-versus-neighbour comparison needs a confidence interval and a pre-specified comparison. In the recording case the issue is a hidden selection rule: if 60 per cent of clusters were excluded, the surviving population has a composition determined by the criterion, and because interspike-interval violation counts scale steeply with firing rate, an absolute threshold removes fast-firing units preferentially. The shared diagnosis is that each paper reports a number that has been optimised by an undisclosed decision and then treats that number as a property of the brain, which is why both need the bounding quantity, namely the selection rule and its effect, to be reported alongside the headline figure.

questions.prompt: A study reports that a polygenic score for a behavioural trait correlates with a brain imaging measure at r equal to 0.15 in 8,000 participants, that the imaging measure correlates with the behaviour at r equal to 0.2, and concludes that the imaging measure mediates the genetic influence. Which elements of this argument are quantitatively and conceptually weak?
questions.answer: Both correlations correspond to 2.25 and 4 per cent of variance, so the measures are largely independent of the predictors and of each other, a mediation claim requires the product of the paths and a test of the indirect effect, and the imaging measure's reliability attenuates the observed associations so the true genetic effect may exceed what was detected.
questions.distractor: The argument is weak only because 8,000 participants are too few for a genetic study, given that complete discovery of the architecture of brain traits requires sample sizes in the millions.
questions.correction: The sample-size point is real but it is about the overall genetic architecture rather than about this specific argument, and correcting it would not repair the inference. The quantitative weakness is that the correlations are tiny: squaring 0.15 and 0.2 gives about 2.25 and 4 per cent of variance, and a mediation chain through two such paths can account for less than a tenth of a per cent of the variance in the outcome under the simplest model, which places it well below the noise floor of most designs and makes the indirect effect estimate unstable. The conceptual weakness is independent: mediation requires temporal ordering and the exclusion of alternative structures, none of which a cross-sectional correlation matrix can provide, and with genetics the exposure precedes everything only in the sense that the genotype is fixed, not that the measured intermediate precedes the outcome. The reliability point adds a direction of correction rather than a criticism of the study's arithmetic, since attenuation means the true associations may be larger than those reported, which is a reminder that unreliable measures cap the inferences available rather than producing false positives.

questions.prompt: You have one month and a fixed budget to test whether a specific cell population is necessary for a behaviour. Choose between a chemogenetic suppression study with 30 animals per group and an optogenetic suppression study with 15 animals per group performed within subjects, and justify the choice with an explicit account of the artifacts each design must bound.
questions.answer: Prefer the within-subject optogenetic design if the behaviour can be measured repeatedly, because within-subject comparison removes between-animal variance and raises power at the same sample, at the cost of adding sham illumination, a temperature estimate and ideally an ion-swapped opsin; the chemogenetic design requires fewer technical controls per animal but needs additional groups for receptor-free and vehicle conditions and a dose-response, which will consume the 30 animals before the question is asked.
questions.distractor: Prefer the chemogenetic design, because it avoids the heating problem entirely and therefore requires fewer controls, making it the cheaper way to establish necessity.
questions.correction: The claim that chemogenetics avoids artifacts rather than substituting different ones is the error to correct. Both tools need specificity evidence, but the evidence differs in kind: for illumination, the artifacts are thermal and ion-specific, bounded by a sham condition, a temperature estimate of roughly 0.067 degrees Celsius per milliwatt and an ion-swapped opsin; for systemic ligand, the artifacts are pharmacological, and the documented conversion of the commonly used ligand into a compound with a broad receptor profile makes a receptor-free group at the same dose and a dose-response mandatory rather than optional. The design choice should then be made on the basis of the behaviour's repeatability and the timescale of the claim: a within-subject optogenetic design can measure responses repeatedly in the same animals and is the better use of 15 animals per group for an acute necessity claim, whereas a chemogenetic suppression is the better fit for a behaviour that unfolds over tens of minutes but cannot test timing, so its extra control groups buy a different claim rather than a stronger one.

questions.prompt: Two years from now, a laboratory publishes a study of adult human hippocampal neurogenesis using tissue from the same donors analysed through both a fresh frozen protocol and a standard fixed protocol, with two immaturity markers, morphology criteria and pre-registered counting rules. The result is that the fixed protocol detects almost no young neurons while the fresh frozen protocol detects a small number. What is the correct interpretation, and what would remain unresolved?
questions.answer: The result identifies processing as a sufficient explanation for at least part of the historical discordance, since the difference appears within the same donors, and it leaves the functional question unresolved: whether the detected cells are functionally integrated young neurons, whether their number has any behavioural consequence, and whether measures from different protocols can be pooled.
questions.distractor: The result settles the debate in favour of the positive studies, because cells detected under conditions that preserve messenger RNA are real while cells lost to fixation were never there to be counted.
questions.correction: The second reading contains the fallacy this level exists to teach, namely moving from a methodological explanation to a biological verdict. A within-donor difference between protocols establishes that processing changes detection, which is a large step forward because it converts an inter-study disagreement into an intra-study comparison, but it does not by itself establish that the cells visible in the preserving protocol are functionally integrated neurons, and the negative studies' own argument was about identification rather than solely about preservation. What remains unresolved is therefore specific and listable: the identity of the counted cells under morphology and independent markers, the relationship between the number of such cells and any functional or behavioural measure, the comparability of counts across protocols, and whether the small number detected is compatible with the daily-addition estimates from birthdating. A field that has made the disagreement procedural has not thereby settled the biology, and the next study should be designed around those four questions rather than around another head-to-head protocol comparison.

questions.prompt: A theory paper argues that a specific dendritic nonlinearity implements a Bayesian inference scheme, showing that a model with this nonlinearity reproduces three published sets of findings. Which additions would turn this into a constraining claim rather than a description, and how would you test them?
questions.answer: The model must make a prediction about a measurement not used in its construction, the prediction must be tested at a stated generalisation level in held-out data, and the comparison must be against a rival model that fits the existing findings equally well but predicts differently, with the discriminating experiment then run using a manipulation that separates the two mechanisms.
questions.distractor: The model must be fitted to more findings, across more brain regions and more species, until the number of reproduced results is large enough that the account can be treated as established.
questions.correction: Adding reproduced findings increases the number of descriptions without increasing the claim's risk, since a model that is flexible enough to reproduce everything constrains little; the source for this lesson states the point directly, that the significant performance of a single model does not strongly constrain theory and that many models must be tested and inferentially compared. What changes a model's status is exposure to refutation, which requires three things in combination. First, a prediction about a measurement that was not used in fitting, at a stated level of generalisation, for instance new stimuli from the same distribution or a new population. Second, a rival, since a model evaluated alone has no evidentiary competition. Third, a discriminating manipulation, because reproducing a phenomenon is compatible with several mechanisms, and only an intervention that separates their predictions can identify which one operates; that is the role the causal tools of this level play. A theory paper that supplies those three would be doing something a theory paper rarely does, and it would be worth the effort.

questions.prompt: Compare two mechanistic claims: that a dendritic plateau potential depolarises the soma enough to influence spike output, and that an astrocyte calcium microdomain triggers gliotransmitter release that changes a synapse. Both rest on measured signals and both involve a step from signal to effect. What distinguishes their evidential standing, and what does each need to be comparable?
questions.answer: The dendritic case has a measured downstream consequence in the same preparation, namely a sustained somatic depolarisation of 10 to 20 millivolts from a local event, whereas the glial case requires an unevidenced intermediate release step whose most-used evidence was challenged by a documented tool-specificity defect, so the astrocyte claim needs an independent demonstration of release plus a neuronal-side manipulation, while the dendritic claim needs a demonstration that the depolarisation changes behaviour.
questions.distractor: The two are equivalent in standing because both are mechanistic claims about a measured signal producing a downstream effect, and in both cases the link would be established in the same way, namely by repeating the measurement in more preparations.
questions.correction: The equivalence claim misses the difference between a chain whose links are measured and a chain whose central link is contested. In the dendritic case the measurement itself spans the link in question: voltage-sensitive dye imaging reports a local event and the same study records the somatic depolarisation it causes, so the propagation step is observed rather than inferred, and the remaining gap is behavioural, which requires perturbation. In the glial case the measured signal is calcium, and the release of a transmitter that acts on the neuron is a separate step whose principal genetic evidence was shown to be confounded by a targeting defect, with the reported modulation of 20 to 30 per cent sitting at the same size as the plausible artifact, so the release step requires independent demonstration rather than repetition. Making the two comparable would require the astrocyte claim to gain a demonstration of release with quantified targeting specificity and a manipulation on the neuronal side, and the dendritic claim to gain a behavioural consequence of the depolarisation.

questions.prompt: A trainee proposes a study with these features: 12 animals per group, optogenetic activation of a projection at 25 milliwatts, no sham illumination group, chemogenetic suppression at 10 milligrams per kilogram of ligand with vehicle controls only, one anatomical marker for cell identity, and analysis of 14 behavioural outcomes with the significant ones reported. Reprioritise the study's resources and give the three changes that would most improve what it can conclude.
questions.answer: Move resources from the number of outcomes to the controls and the sample: power the design for a stated minimum effect of interest, roughly 63 animals per group for a 0.5 standard deviation effect at 80 per cent power, add the sham and temperature controls plus a receptor-free ligand group, and pre-specify one primary outcome with the remaining outcomes labelled exploratory, because 14 uncorrected tests carry a family-wise error rate above 0.5 and the current design risks concluding nothing from any of them.
questions.distractor: Keep the design and add more anatomical markers for cell identity, since the credibility of a circuit claim rests on demonstrating that the manipulated cells are the intended population and the behavioural outcomes are secondary.
questions.correction: Marker validation is worth doing and is a small fix, but it cannot rescue a study whose inferential budget has been spent on outcomes rather than on controls. The arithmetic of multiplicity makes that concrete: 14 independent tests at an alpha of 0.05 give a family-wise error rate of one minus 0.95 to the fourteenth power, which is above 0.5, so the procedure is more likely than not to produce at least one false positive, and reporting only the significant outcomes converts that probability into a published claim. At the same time, 12 animals per group has about 20 per cent power for a 0.5 standard deviation effect, so a null would be uninformative. The three changes that matter most are therefore a pre-specified primary outcome with a stated correction for the secondary ones, a sample sized for the smallest effect that would change the conclusion, and the artifact controls the tools require, namely sham illumination and a temperature estimate alongside an opsin-free comparison, and a receptor-free ligand group because the systemic ligand acts substantially through a conversion product; the ion-swapped opsin comparison is a lower priority than those, and additional markers are worth adding only after the rest is fixed.
